title: Master Mason: traditional history and concluding signs
summary: Read the remainder of the Hiram narrative and the source’s concluding material.

sections.heading: Refreshment and return
sections.body:
Calling the Brethren from Labour to Refreshment.
(The W.M. gives one knock, which is answered by the Wardens.)
W. M. - Principal Officers upstanding.
(The Wardens rise with the W.M.)
W. M. - Bro. Junior Warden, (J.W. responds with and holds the sign of E.A.) what time is it?
J. W. - High Noon, Worshipful Master.
W. M. - What is to be done at High Noon?
J. W. - Your Worship's pleasure.
W. M. - Then you will call the Brethren from labour to refreshment.
(J.W. discharges sign of E.A.)
J. W. - Brethren, it is the Worshipful Master's command that you cease from labour and go to refreshment; taking care to keep within hail, so as to be ready to come on again in due time, that profit and pleasure may be the result.
(The J.W. gives one knock, which is repeated by the S.W. and the W.M. The J.W. raises his Column, the S.W. lowers his. The I.P.M. closes the V.S.L., without moving the Square and Compasses.)
Calling the Brethren from Refreshment to Labour.
(The W.M. gives one knock, which is repeated by the Wardens.)
W. M. - Principal Officers upstanding.
(The Wardens rise with the W.M.)
W. M. - Bro. Junior Warden, (J.W. responds with and holds the sign of E.A.) what time is it?
J. W. - Past High Noon, Worshipful Master.
W. M. - Then you will call the Brethren from refreshment to labour.
(J.W. discharges sign of E.A.)
J. W. - Brethren, it is the Worshipful Master's command that you cease from refreshment and return to labour, for the further despatch of Masonic business.
(The J.W. gives one knock which is repeated by the S.W. and the W.M. The J.W. lowers his Column, and the S.W. raises his. The I.P.M. reopens the V.S.L.)

sections.heading: The second part and traditional history
sections.body:
The Ceremony of Raising to the Third Degree ( 2nd Part )
(The Can. is restored to his former comforts and wearing a M.M. apron. The Tyler gives the knocks of the 3rd Degree.)
J. W. - (rises with step and sign of a M.M.) Worshipful Master, there is a report. (J.W. holds sign.)
W. M. - Bro. Junior Warden, you will inquire who seeks admission. Should it be the return of our newly raised Master Mason, admit him. (J.W. discharges sign and sits down.)
J. W. - Bro. Inner Guard, (I.G. responds and holds sign of a M.M.) you will see who seeks admission. Should it be the return of our newly raised Master Mason, admit him.
(The I.G. discharges sign and opens the door.)
I. G. - (to Tyler) Whom have you there?
TY. - Our newly raised Master Mason.
(The S.D. squares the Lodge via the East, South and joined by the J.D. together goes to the door. The S.D. conducts the Can. to the N.W. corner of the Lodge and places him facing East with right hand over left breast.)
S. D. - You will salute the Worshipful Master with the step and sign of a Master Mason.
(The S.D. conducts the Can. down South and stops at about mid- point between the North-West corner and the Secretary’s table and places him facing South looking towards the S.W.)
(The S.W. rises and salutes the W.M. as a M.M.)
S. W. - (to Deacons) Bro. Deacons, please be seated. (Deacons sit down.)
S. W. - (to Can.) We discontinued the narrative of our Traditional History at that part of it which describes the manner of the Death of the Grand Master, Hiram Abif. A loss so important as that of the Chief Architect could not fail to be speedily and severely felt. The want of those plans and designs which had theretofore been regularly supplied through every department of the work, had given rise to grave apprehensions that some serious mischance must have befallen him. The Menatschim - who were the general Overseers of the work - deputed certain of the more distinguished of their number to crave an audience with King Solomon, and to acquaint him with the utter confusion into which the absence of the Chief Architect had plunged them, and at the same time to express to him their fears that to some dire calamity must be attributed his so sudden and mysterious disappearance. King Solomon thereupon ordered a general muster of the Craftsmen throughout the various departments, when three of the superior class were not to be found; and on the same day the two who had originally joined in the conspiracy went before the King, and made a full confession of all that they knew, up to the time of their withdrawing themselves from the number of the conspirators. The fears of King Solomon being awakened for the safety of the Chief Architect, he selected fifteen trusty Fellow-Crafts, and ordered them to go and make diligent search for the person of the Grand Master, and to ascertain if he were still or had suffered in the attempt to extort from him the Secrets of his superior Degree. Accordingly, a day having been fixed for their return to Jerusalem, they formed themselves into three Fellow-Craft Lodges, consisting of five each, and departed severally from the three entrances of the Temple. Many days were spent in fruitless search; indeed, one Lodge eventually returned to Jerusalem without having effected any discovery; but the Brethren of the Second Lodge were more fortunate, for on the evening of a certain day, they having suffered many privations and much personal fatigue, one of their number, who had rested himself in a reclining position, in order to assist his rising, took hold of a shrub under whose shade he had reclined, and which to his surprise came easily out of the ground. On a close examination of the spot he discovered that the surface had been recently disturbed; he therefore hailed his Brethren, and with their assistance he reopened the ground, and there discovered the body of the Grand Master, very indecently buried. They covered it up with all respect and reverence; and in order to mark the spot they placed a branch of acacia at the head of the grave and then hastened to com- municate the afflicting intelligence to King Solomon. He, when the first emotions of his grief had subsided, ordered them to return, taking with them a sufficient number of Brethren to assist them, and to raise the body of Hiram Abif and to convey it to Jerusalem, there to perform upon it such rites of sepulture as became his rank and exalted talents. At the same time he informed them that by his untimely death the Genuine Secrets of a Master Mason were for a time Lost ; he therefore charged them to be particularly careful to observe any Casual Sign, Token, or Word which might occur while they were engaged in performing this last sad office of respect to departed merit. They performed their task with the utmost fidelity, for, on reopening the grave, one of the Brethren, looking round, observed several standing in this position, as though struck with Horror (sign) at what they beheld; others, viewing the gaping wound still visible on his forehead smote their own thus in Sympathy (sign) with his Sufferings. Two of the Brethren then descended into the grave, and severally attempted to raise the body of the Grand Master by the Grip of an Entered Apprentice and a Fellow-Craft; but as the body had lain some days in the Grave the Flesh gave and Slipped. A third zealous and more expert Brother then descended and taking a Firm and Lion-Like hold on the Sinew of the Right Arm, he, with the assistance of the other two, succeeded in raising him on the Five Points Of Fellowship and while some looked on in speechless Grief, others more animated exclaimed, Machaben and Machbinna, these Words signifying severally the Death of the Builder and the Builder is Slain. These Casual Signs, Grip, and Words were duly reported to King Solomon, who whereupon ordered that they should serve to distinguish them and all Master Masons throughout the World, until time or circumstances should restore the genuine ones. It only remains for me to account for the Third Lodge of Craftsmen. They had pursued their researches in the direction of Joppa, and were meditating a return to Jerusalem, when, on passing the mouth of a cavern, they heard issuing therefrom sounds of lamentation and remorse. On entering to ascertain the cause, they found three men who appeared to answer the description of those who were missing, and who on being charged with the murder, and finding all chance of escape cut off, made a full confession of their guilt. They were then Bound and Led to Jerusalem, where King Solomon ordered them to immediate execution, a punishment which the heinousness of their crime richly merited. The Body of Hiram Abif was ordered to be Reburied near to, but without, the walls of Jerusalem. He could not be buried within the precincts of the Temple, nor even within the City, because during the forty years' wanderings of the Israelites in the Wilderness, they, by God's special command, buried their dead beyond (or outside) the limits of the Camp; and when they entered into the Promised Land, and dwelt in fenced cities, they always buried their dead without the walls of their several cities. The fifteen Trusty Fellow-Crafts who had assisted in searching and finding the body of the Grand Master and in bringing his murderers to justice, were ordered to conduct his obsequies, clothed in White Aprons as emblems of their innocence. The implements with which Hiram Abif was Slain are the Plump Rule, the Level, and the Heavy Maul. The Skull and Cross Bones the emblems of mortality, are intended to remind us of his Untimely Death, which took place about three thousand years after the date commonly assigned to the creation of the world. (S.W. salutes the W.M. as a M.M. and sits.)

sections.heading: Concluding signs and the Royal Arch reference
sections.body:
(The S.D. conducts the Can. to the North/North-East corner of the Lodge and places Can. facing South.)
P. M. - You have already been put into possession of the three ordinary Sign of a Master Mason; I will now intrust you with the remaining two; but for your further instruction I will go through the whole five. This (P.M. demonstrates) is the Sign of Horror; this (P.M. demonstrates) is the Sign of Sympathy; this (P.M. demonstrates) is the Penal Sign. The fourth is the Sign of Grief and Distress. The origin of this Sign was the gesture made by Hiram Abif when after the second blow he made his way from the North to the East Entrance of the Temple, when his distress and agony were so great that the sweat and blood stood in great drops upon his fore- head, and he used this Sign (P.M. demonstrates) as a temporary alleviation of his sufferings. There is another Sign of Grief and Distress said to be in use in certain countries on the Continent of Europe, and which may be useful to a Brother who may happen to be in danger or difficulty in any of those countries. It is given by Clasping the Hands together thus with the Palms outwards, the Hands raised to the Forehead and exclaiming aloud in the language of the country, ‘Come to my assistance, ye Sons of the Widow’ You have already been informed that Hiram Abif was the Son of a Widow of Tyre and as we all masonically claim brotherhood with Hiram Abif so we may all be designated Sons of the Widow.
The fifth in order is the Grand and Royal Sign. It had its origin at the time when the Queen of Sheba, attended by her brilliant retinue, went to view the buildings of the Temple, when they were all so struck by their exceeding magnificence, that raising their Hands above their Heads and bringing the Palms together in the Oriental manner (thus), they exclaimed as with one voice, ‘Oh, Wonderful Masons’
(At a signal from the P.M. the W.M. gives one knock follow by the S.W. and J.W.)
W. M. - To order, Brethren. (the brethren all rise)
P. M. - But King Solomon and those who were present with him, in humble acknowledgment that that great and holy work had been carried on and completed, only through the guidance and the strengthening power of the Almighty; and desiring to ascribe to Him alone the praise and honour and glory, raised their hands in like manner, and exclaimed in unison, 'All Glory to the Most High.'
(All the Brethren accompany the W.M. in act and in word.)
W. M. - Brethren, be seated.
(The S.D. conducts the Can. to the front of the W.M.’s pedestal.)
W. M. - (to Can.) This is the conclusion of the Third Ceremony. At the expiration of a full month, or at any time after that period, you may, if you wish it, be admitted to the Degree of the Holy Royal Arch, the only Degree above the Craft that is recognised by, and is under the sanction of, the Grand Lodge of England.
(S.D. places Can. one pace back and instructs Can.)
S. D. - You will salute the W.M. as a M.M. (Can. does so and S.D. conducts the Can. to any seat in the Lodge except the East. The Deacons return to the respective positions, place the wands in the stands and sit in unison.)
END OF THE CEREMONY OF THE THIRD DEGREE

title: Master Mason: closing and return to the first degree
summary: Follow the final transitions and closing sequence in the supplied text.

sections.heading: Short closing to the first degree
sections.body:
The Ceremony of Closing the Lodge in the Third Degree. ( short closing to First Degree )
(The W. M. rises and gives one knock with his gavel which is answered by the Wardens.)
W. M. - Brethren, assist me to close the Lodge in the Third Degree. (All rise.)
W. M. - Bro. Junior Warden, (J.W. responds with step and sign of M.M.) what is the constant care of every Master Mason?
J. W. - To prove the Lodge close tyled.
W. M. - You will direct that duty to be done. (J.W. discharges sign.)
J. W. - Bro. Inner Guard, (I.G. responds with step and sign of M.M.) you will prove the Lodge close tyled.
(The I.G. discharges sign, goes to the door and gives the 3rd Degree knocks, which are answered by the Ty.)
I. G. (with step and sign of M.M. )
Bro. Junior Warden, the Lodge is close tyled. (I.G. discharges sign.)
J. W. (with step and sign of M.M. )
Worshipful Master, the Lodge is close tyled. (J.W. discharges sign.)
W. M. - Bro. Senior Warden, (S.W. responds with step and sign of M.M.) what is our next care ?
S. W. - To see that the Brethren appear to order as Master Masons.
W. M. - Brethren, to order in the Third Degree. (All stand to order.)
W. M. - Brethren, by the powers invested in me, I close this Master Masons degree and resume labour in the First Degree. (At the word ‘close’, all the Brethren drop the sign in unison with the W.M. He gives the knocks of the First Degree.)
(W,M. gives the First Degree knocks, followed by the S.W., J.W., I.G. and the Ty.)
I.P.M. goes to the W.M.’s pedestal, kneel on his left knee and conceal both points of the Compasses. I.P.M. salutes the W.M. as an E.A. and returns to his seat.)

sections.heading: Final closing of the lodge
sections.body:
The Ceremony of Closing the Lodge.
(The W.M. rises and gives one knock which is answered by the S.W. and the J.W.)
W. M. - Brethren, assist me to close the Lodge. (All rise.)
W. M. - Bro. Junior Warden, (J.W. responds with and holds the sign of E.A.) what is the constant care of every Freemason?
J. W. - To prove the Lodge close tyled.
W. M. - You will direct that duty to be done. (J.W. discharges the sign of E.A.)
J. W. - Bro. Inner Guard, (I.G. responds with and holds the sign of E.A.) you will prove the Lodge close tyled.
(The I.G. discharges sign of E.A. and gives the 3 knocks, which are answered by the Tyler.)
I. G. - (with step and sign of E.A.) Bro. Junior Warden, the Lodge is close tyled
. J. W. - (rises with step and sign of E.A.) Worshipful Master, the Lodge is close tyled.
W. M. - Bro. Senior Warden, (S.W. responds with and holds the sign of E.A.) what is our next care ?
S. W. - To see that the Brethren appear to order as Freemasons. (S.W. discharges the sign of E.A.)
W. M. - Brethren, to order as Freemasons.
(All stand to order as E.A.) W. M. - Bro. Senior Warden, your constant place in the Lodge?
S. W. - In the West.
W. M. - Why are you so placed?
S. W. - As the sun sets in the West to close the day, so the Senior Warden is placed in the West to close the Lodge by the Worshipful Master's command, after having seen that every Brother has had his due.
Chaplain - Brethren, before the Lodge is closed, let us with all reverence and humility express our gratitude to The Great Architect Of The Universe for the favours which we have received, and may He continue to preserve our Order by adorning its members with every moral and social virtue. So Mote It Be.
W. M. - Bro. Senior Warden, the labours of the day being ended, you have my command to close the Lodge.
(W.M. maintains the sign ; gives one knock with the left hand.)
S. W. - Brethren, by command of the Worshipful Master, I close the Lodge.
(At the word ' close,' all drop the sign in unison. The S.W. gives one knock. The J.D. goes to the Secretary’s table and the S.D. goes to the J.W.’s pedestal. I.P.M. goes to the centre of the Lodge under the ‘G’. Deacons cross their wands with a click to signal the I.P.M. to walk to the W.M.’s pedestal escorted by the Deacons with wands crossed. I.P.M. kneel on his left knee and close the V.S.L. and place the Square and Compasses on it. I.P.M. gives a court bow to the W.M. and returns to his seat. Both Deacons give court bow and return to their respective positions and place their wands in the stands. J.D. closes the first degree tracing board and S.D. puts out the candle on W.M.’s pedestal. S.W. and J.W. put out their candles and S.W. lowers his column to a horizontal position.)
J. W. - And it is closed accordingly until the fourth Wednesday in the ensuing month, except in case of emergency, of which due notice will be given.
(J.W. gives one knock, followed by the I.G. and the Tyler. J.W. raises his column to an upright position.)
I. P. M. (steps down to the floor of the Lodge in front of the W.M.’s pedestal and places his right hand on the closed V.S.L.)
Brethren, nothing now remains but, according to ancient custom, that each Brother lock up the secrets of the Lodge in the safe and sacred repository, the heart, uniting in the act of Fidelity, Fidelity, Fidelity (all give sign of fidelity 3 times), and may God be with us all. So Mote It Be.
(All Brethren remain standing while the D. of C. leads the J.D. from his position, follow by the S.D. taking his position on the J.D.’s left, then the J.W. taking his position behind the Deacons, then the S.W. taking his position on the J.W.’s left and then the W.M. taking his position behind the Deacons and in front of the Wardens. Deacons cross the wands at the door for the W.M. and Wardens to pass under.

title: Freemasonry: how to read the supplied rituals
summary: Understand the three-degree sequence, roles, abbreviations and limits of this particular transcript.

sections.heading: What the collection contains
sections.body:
Thirteen linked readings retain all 1,036 source paragraphs across the Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft and Master Mason sections. Repeated openings and closings remain in their original place. The supporting explanations on this page are editorial additions.
The ritual names Centenary Lodge and refers to the Grand Lodge of England. Those internal references suggest an English-related setting, but they do not establish the document’s author, date, official status or exact ritual tradition. The Royal Arch is named, not supplied as an additional ceremony.

sections.heading: Reading the page
sections.body:
Speaker labels identify the person speaking. Directions in parentheses describe the supplied staging. Abbreviated words and dotted blanks stay as they appear; some words withheld in one passage are written fully elsewhere. No blanks have been completed from outside material.
Biblical episodes, architectural imagery and the Hiram narrative should be read as elements of this ritual text. A symbol’s appearance is not evidence for allegations that an organization secretly controls unrelated events.

sections.heading: Officers and abbreviations
sections.body:
W.M. means Worshipful Master; S.W. and J.W. are Senior and Junior Warden; S.D. and J.D. are Senior and Junior Deacon; I.G. is Inner Guard; TY. is Tyler.
I.P.M. is Immediate Past Master; P.M. is Past Master; D. of C. is Director of Ceremonies; A.D. of C. is Assistant Director of Ceremonies. CAN. denotes the candidate, SEC. the secretary, and V.S.L. the Volume of Sacred Law. M.M. may denote Master Mason or a member delivering a passage, depending on context.
E.A., F.C. and M.M. also identify the three degrees. The source’s membership wording belongs to its particular setting; UGLE’s public FAQ separately recognizes women’s Grand Lodges, so the transcript should not be treated as an exhaustive description of all Freemasonry.

The first degree discusses time, conscience and education; the second discusses moral conduct, equality and uprightness; the third connects the skirret, pencil and compasses with a straight course of conduct, accountability and limits.

sections.body:

The Hiram narrative makes fidelity, loss and mortality central to the third degree. The five points of fellowship are explained as mutual assistance and lawful confidentiality; the source itself excepts crimes from that confidentiality.

The supplied labels are Keter/Crown, Chochma/Wisdom, Binah/Understanding, Chesed/Loving Kindness, Gevurah/Strength, Tiferet/Beauty, Netzach/Victory, Hod/Empathy, Yesod/Foundation and Malkhut/Sovereignty. Transliteration and English interpretation vary; these are the labels visible in this image.

title: Read a claim: source, interpretation and evidence
summary: Use a simple reading framework for mixed historical, spiritual and conspiracy material.

sections.heading: Start with the claim, not the whole web
sections.body:
Choose one statement with identifiable actors, dates and actions. Find the original document, understand what it actually says, and check whether independent evidence supports the conclusion. Hundreds of neighboring names do not strengthen an unsupported connecting arrow.
Keep four distinctions visible: the creator’s work, the creator’s interpretation, the evidence for a particular statement, and the reader’s unanswered question. A primary source for an artwork is not necessarily an evidential source for its allegations.

sections.heading: Different labels for different material
sections.body:
Documented record means an identifiable record supports the particular event. Religious or symbolic interpretation describes meaning within a tradition. Hypothesis or speculation describes a proposal not established by the supplied evidence. Unsupported allegation means the upload does not substantiate the accusation. Contradicted or fabricated is used where specific reliable evidence justifies that stronger conclusion.
For example, the Senate hearing is evidence for historical MKUltra investigations. It does not validate every mind-control narrative. The Protocols of the Elders of Zion is an antisemitic fabrication, not a missing document that would prove collective Jewish control.

sections.heading: Follow the limits through the page
sections.body: Image captions identify creators, uploaded versions, uncertainties and source links. They do not certify the charts. Some fine print is difficult to read in the supplied raster images; a transcription should never turn an uncertain label into an invented fact.

sections.heading: Deep State: the source heading
sections.body:
Seven charts follow this heading in the document, but they are not all by the same creator and do not all address the same subject. This page handles four power/history maps; the Great Awakening and health-related works have their own guides.

sections.heading: Four maps, different provenance
sections.body:
The uploaded color key and black-and-white Q-Web are related Dylan Louis Monroe artworks. The Cult of Baal uses a different symbolic historical arrangement. The World Government image is a 2005 work by Bureau d’Études. Their visual proximity in the upload does not establish a shared research method or independent corroboration.
Each source panel below links to the creator’s own publication or catalogue. An uploaded edition is identified separately from later artwork currently shown on those sites. Exact historical download-file matches are not claimed where they have not been established.

sections.heading: How to follow a connection
sections.body:
Identify whether a line means ownership, a meeting, influence, chronology, a symbol or simply the artist’s proposed connection. Then locate evidence for that exact relation. A real institution, historical abuse or family relationship does not prove every further inference drawn from it.
The supplied image files remain available for close reading in bounded, collapsible panels; no dense chart is stretched across the article as an unexplained background. Creator links are sources for attribution, not endorsements or guarantees of the claims.

title: The Great Awakening Map: spiritual and disclosure narratives
summary: Read Parinya Champ’s map as an attributed worldview combining spirituality, extraordinary claims and political narratives.

sections.heading: Read by theme
sections.body:
The upper area emphasizes consciousness, meditation, liberation and spiritual ascent. Other regions connect extraterrestrial narratives, alleged hidden technology, ancient civilizations and political claims. These themes should be explored separately rather than accepted as one explanatory system.
The artist’s 2018 publications identify the project and describe its worldview. They establish authorship and context, not independent proof of the phenomena or future events the map proposes.

sections.heading: Keep interpretation and measurement separate
sections.body: A spiritual teaching can be discussed in its own religious context. A claim that a stellar event transforms human bodies or that a concealed fleet operates in space requires a separate evidential argument. Neither follows merely from the presence of sacred geometry or scientific vocabulary.

sections.heading: Pricing objectives, costs, markups and value approaches

Price
Price is the amount of money charged for a product or service; the sum of the values that consumers exchange for the benefits of having or using the product or service
Price is the only element in the marketing mix that produces revenue; all other elements represent costs
How we Benchmark
Pricing Objectives
Sales Maximisation
Profit Maximisation
No demand for product greater than its value
No profit if priced below cost
Pricing Methods
Cost-based pricing
Involves setting prices based on the costs for producing, distributing and selling the product plus a fair rate of return for effort and risk
Fixed costs (overheads)
The costs that do not vary with production or sales level
Rent
Heat
Interest
Executive salaries
Variable costs
Costs that vary directly with the level of production
Packaging
Raw materials
Total costs
The sum of the fixed and variable costs for any given level of production
Cost-plus pricing
Adds a standard markup to the cost of the product
Benefits
Sellers are certain about costs
Prices are similar in industry and price competition is minimised
Buyers feel it is fair
Disadvantages
Ignores demand and competitor prices

Setting prices based on competitors’ strategies, prices, costs and market offerings.
Consumers will base their judgements of a product’s value on the prices that competitors charge for similar products
Customer value-based pricing
Understanding how much value consumers place on the benefits they receive from the product and setting a price that captures that value
Value-based pricing
Uses the buyers’ perceptions of value, not the seller’s cost, as the key to pricing. Price is considered before the marketing programme is set
Value-based pricing is customer driven
Cost-based pricing is product driven
Good-value pricing
Offers the right combination of quality and good service at a fair price
Everyday low pricing (EDLP)
Involves charging a constant everyday low price with few or no temporary price discounts
High–low pricing
Involves charging higher prices on an everyday basis but running frequent promotions to lower prices temporarily on selected items

Attaches value-added features and services to differentiate a company’s offers and charging higher prices

Terms
Product
A product is anything we can offer to a market for attention, acquisition, use, or consumption that might satisfy a need or want.
It may be a physical good, a service, a retail outlet, a person, an organization, a place, or even an idea.
5 Levels of meanings for a product
Core benefit
The fundamental need or want that consumers satisfy by consuming the product or service.
E.g. Cooling and comfort
Generic product
A basic version of the product containing only those attributes or characteristics absolutely necessary for its functioning but with no distinguishing features.
E.g. Sufficient cooling capacity, an acceptable energy efficiency rating, adequate air intakes and exhausts, etc.
Expected product
A set of attributes or characteristics that buyers normally expect and agree to when they purchase a product.
E.g. Consumer Reports states that for a typical large air conditioner, consumers should expect at least two cooling speeds, expandable plastic side panels, adjustable louvers, removable air filter, vent for exhausting air, power cord at least 60 inches long, R-22 HCFC refrigerant, etc.
Augmented product
Includes additional product attributes, benefits, or related services that distinguish the product from competitors.
E.g. Optional features may include electric touch-pad controls, a display to show indoor and outdoor temperatures and the thermostat setting, an automatic mode to adjust fan speed based on the thermostat setting and room temperature, a toll free 800 number for customer service, etc.
Potential product
Includes all the augmentations and transformations that a product might ultimately undergo in the future.
E.g. Silent running, completely balanced throughout the room, and energy self sufficient

Brand recognition
Refers to consumer’s ability to correctly discriminate the brand as having been seen or heard before.
E.g. have you heard of Tesla?

In basic procedures consumers are given items (orally or visually) and are asked about their knowledge of such items

Brand recall
Relates to consumer’s ability to retrieve the brand form memory when given the product category, the needs fulfilled by the category, a purchase or consumption situation
E.g. think of a soft drink. Was it a Coke?

Clarify brand awareness

sections.heading: Extension types and Tauber’s category routes
sections.body:
Brand Extension
When a firm uses an established brand name to introduce a new product
The parent brand is the brand that gives birth to a brand extension
The sub-brand is the new brand resulting from the extension
Brand extension classification
Line extension: using a sub-brand to target a new market segment within the same product category
Category extension: using the parent brand in a different product category

Introduce the same product in a different form
Introduce products that contain the brand’s distinctive taste, ingredient, or component
Introduce companion products for the brand
Introduce products relevant to the customer franchise of the brand
Introduce products that capitalize on the firm’s perceived expertise

sections.heading: Knowledge, fit, leverage and launch evaluation
sections.body:
Management Process
Brand knowledge
Brand awareness of the parent brand
What is its depth?
What is its breadth?
Brand associations of the parent brand
Focus: attributes / benefits / values?
Their strength / favorability / uniqueness?
Perceptual fit
The degree of similarity between the parent brand and the extension
It can occur at the level of product category (category fit) or brand associations (brand fit)
Product-feature similarity vs. brand concept consistency
Function-oriented brands vs. prestige-oriented brands
Benefit transfer
The process through which the benefits associated to the parent brand are transferred to the extension brand
Are these benefits transferable?
Competitive leverage
It refers to the ability of the extension brand to be perceived as relevant and differentiating in the new category
Can the extension brand achieve points of parity and points of difference?
Can the extension brand achieve a competitive advantage?
Steps in introducing brand extensions successfully
Define actual and desired consumer knowledge about the brand (e.g., create a mental map and identify sources of equity)
Identify possible extension candidates on basis of parent brand associations and overall similarity or fit of extension to the parent brand
Evaluate the potential of the extension candidate to create equity according to the three-factor model
Salience of parent brand associations
Favorability of inferred extension associations
Uniqueness of inferred extension associations
Evaluate extension candidate feedback effects according to the four-factor model:
How compelling the extension evidence is
How relevant the extension evidence is

How strong the extension evidence is
Consider possible competitive advantages as perceived by consumers and possible reactions initiated by consumers
Design marketing campaign to launch extension

sections.heading: Potential advantages and disadvantages
sections.body:
Advantage of extensions
Facilitate new product acceptance
Improve brand image
Reduce risk perceived by customers
Increase the probability of gaining distribution and trial

Reduce costs of introductory and follow-up marketing programs
Avoid cost of developing a new brand

Enhance the parent brand image

Can succeed but hurt the image of the parent brand

sections.heading: Guidelines and their limits
sections.body:
Guidelines
Brand extensions are successful when the parent brand is seen as having favorable associations and there is a perception of fit between the parent and the extension
There are many bases for fit: product-related attributes ad benefits as well as non-product-related attributes and benefits related to common usage or user type
Depending on consumer knowledge of the product categories, perception of fit may be based on technical or manufacturing commonalities or more surface considerations such as necessary or situation complementarity
High-quality brands stretch further that average-quality brands, although both types have boundaries
A brand that is seen as prototypical of a product category can be difficult to extend outside the category
Concrete attribute associations tend to be more difficult to extend than abstract benefit associations
Consumers may transfer associations that are positive in the original product class but become negative in the extension context
Consumers may infer negative associations about an extension, perhaps even based on the inferred positive associations
It can be difficult to extend into a product class that is seen as easy to make
A successful extension can not only contribute to the parent brand image but also enable a brand to be extended even more
An unsuccessful extension hurts the parent brand only when there is a strong basis of fit between the two
An unsuccessful extension does not prevent a firm from backtracking and introducing a more similar extension
Vertical extension can be difficult and often require sub-branding strategies
The most effective advertising strategy for an extension is one that emphasizes information about the extension

title: Choose marketing channels with a Bullseye shortlist

sections.heading: The supplied Bullseye outline
sections.body:
The outer ring is an inventory of possible channels. The empty middle and inner rings invite narrowing that inventory; they do not contain selected winners. Use the experiment sequence below to make and document your own choices rather than reading the numbered slots as a ranking.
Bullseye Framework

sections.heading: Turn the outline into a useful decision
sections.body:
Start with the audience and the outcome you want: awareness, qualified enquiries, purchases or repeat use. Shortlist channels that can plausibly reach that audience and record the assumptions behind each choice.
For each shortlisted channel, define a small experiment, its budget and time window, and the same decision metric where comparison is meaningful. Keep the evidence with the decision; reach and clicks alone do not establish profitable acquisition.
Review results before committing more resources. A channel that works for one audience, offer or stage may fail for another; the source does not prescribe universal winners.

(Income earned vs. expenses incurred) vs. (money in vs. money out).

"Wear and tear" of your fixed assets vs. intangible assets such as goodwill.

Same as Gross Profit vs. Net Profit over revenue.

US standards vs other countries standards.

Estimated current market value of an asset or liability vs. the original purchase price recorded in the books at the time of acquisition.

Acquisition for the intangible attributes and synergies of the acquired company vs. non-physical assets with future economic benefits.

Assets on the balance sheet vs. expenses recorded on the income statement.

Liability that is uncertain in timing or amount vs. company's profits set aside for a specific purpose.

Total par value of shares issued by a company to shareholders vs. accumulated profits kept within the company after paying dividends or losses.
Lease vs. Loan
Involve asset vs. sum of money.

Economically usable by the compan vs. economic benefits, which may extend beyond its useful life.

Specific choice of accounting principles vs. the approximation of uncertain amounts used to recognise transactions.

Matching of the transactions on your bank statement to the transactions in your general ledger.

Expenses already incurred, but have no yet received a bill / paid for.

Amounts paid out, typically to landlords, that are owed back to you at the end of your lease.

Future economic value that has yet to be incurred.
Inventory

Amounts paid to/from a parent and subsidiary.

Interest expense that have not paid out.

Payroll expenses that have not paid out.

sections.heading: Recognition, initial cost and key definitions

An entity shall assess the probability of expected future economic benefits using reasonable and supportable assumptions that represent management’s best estimate of the set of economic conditions that will exist over the useful life of the asset.
The time should meet the definition of an intangible asset

Definitions
Intangible asset
Intangible asset is an identifiable non~monetary asset without physical substance controlled by the entity from which future economic benefits are expected to flow to the entity
Amortisation
Amortisation is the systematic allocation of the depreciable amount of an intangible asset over its useful life.
Asset
An asset is a resource: (a) controlled by an entity as a result of past events; and (b) from which future economic benefits are expected to flow to the entity.
Carrying amount
Carrying amount is the amount at which an asset is recognised in the statement of financial position after deducting any accumulated amortisation and accumulated impairment losses thereon
Cost
Cost is the amount of cash or cash equivalents paid or the fair value of other consideration given to acquire an asset at the time of its acquisition or construction
Development
Development is the application of research findings or other knowledge of a plan or design for the production of new or substantially improved materials, devices, products, processes, systems or services before the start of commercial production or use.
Fair value
Fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date
Research
Research is an original and planned investigation undertaken with the prospect of gaining new scientific or technical knowledge and understanding.
Useful life

sections.heading: Intellectual property and subsequent measurement

Intellectual Property (IP)

Invesment in development
Software, trademarks, brand
IP on lease agreement
Consessions, patents
IP in preparation
Measurement after initial recognition
Cost modelAfter initial recognition, an intangible asset shall be carried at its cost less any accumulated amortisation and any accumulated impairment losses.
Revaluation modelAfter initial recognition, an intangible asset shall be carried at a revalued amount, being its fair value a! the date of the revaluation less any subsequent accumulated amortisation and any subsequent accumulated impairment losses. For the purpose of revaluations under this standard, fair value shall be measured by reference to an active market. Revaluations shall be made with such regularity that at the end of the reporting period lht' carrying amount of the asset does not differ materially from its fair value.
IP carrying amount is increased
Increase shall be recognised in equity under the heading of revaluation surplus. However, the increase shall be recognised in P&L to the extent that it reverses a revaluation decrease of the same asset previously recognised in P&L.
IP carrying amount is decreased
Decrease shall be recognised in P&L. However, the decrease shall be recognised in other comprehensive income to the extent of any credit balance in the revaluation surplus in respect to that asset

sections.heading: Liquidity, working capital and financing
sections.body:
Debt-to-equity
Total debt / total equity
Debt-to-assets
Total debt / total assets
Current ratio
Current assets / current liabilities
Equity multiplier
Total assets / total equity
Quick ratio
(Current assets − inventory − prepayments − other non-quick current assets) / current liabilities
Cash ratio
Cash and cash equivalents / current liabilities
Net working capital
Current assets − current liabilities
Net working capital to total assets
(Current assets − current liabilities) / total assets
Debt-to-capitalisation
Debt / (debt + equity)
Debt-to-Equity Ratio = Total Debt / Total Equity
Amount of debt a company has in relation to its equity. The lower the ratio, the less the debt compared to its equity.
Debt-to-Assets Ratio = Total Debt / Total Asset
Amount of debt a company has in relation to its assets. The lower the ration, the less the debt compared to assets.
Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities
Measures whether a company has enough short-term assets to cover its short-term liabilities. The higher the ratio, the more assets you have in relation to your liabilities.
Equity Multiplier = Total Assets / Total Equity
Measures the proportion of a company's assets that are financed through debt versus equity. A high equity multiplier means the company is relying more on debt to finance it's assets rather than equity.
Quick Ratio = (Current Assets - Inventory) / Current Liabilities
Shows the ability of a company to meet its short-term obligations with its most liquid assets. The high the ratio, the more liquidity your business has.
Cash Ratio = Cash and Cash Equivalent / Current Liabilities
Amount of cash and equivalents a company has in relation to its current liabilities. The higher the ratio, the more cash you have in comparison with your current liabilities.
Net Working capital = Current Assets - Current Liabilities
Short-term liquidity and its ability to meet its current obligations. Higher NWC indicates that the company has a comfortable cushion of liquid assets to cover its short-term liabilities.
Net Working Capital Ratio = (Current Assets - Current Liabilities) / Total Assets
Showcases the difference between a company's current asset and its current liabilities. The higher the ratio, the more current assets you have compared to your current liabilities.
Total Debt-to-Capitalisation Ratio = Total Debt / (Total Debt + Shareholders' Equity)
The total amount of debt in relation to a company's total capitalisation (debt & equity). The lower ratio, the less your business is captailised using debt.

sections.heading: The source’s adjusted tangible-net-worth measure
sections.body:

Total liabilities / (equity − intangibles − prepayments − related-party receivables)
Tangible Net Worth Ratio = Total Liabilities / (Total Equity - Intangible Assets - Prepaid Assets - Due from Related Parties)
The value of all your assets and the size of all your liabilities

sections.heading: Bank capital adequacy: a specialist measure

sections.heading: Returns and turnover measures

Return on assets
Net income / average total assets
Return on equity
Attributable net income / average corresponding equity
Total asset turnover
Net sales / average total assets

Payables turnover

Amount of net income a company generates in relation to its total assets. The higher your RoA, the better your return on your assets.
Return on Equity (RoE) = Net Income / Average Shareholders' Equity
Amount of net income a company generates in relation to its equity. The higher your RoE, the better return you are getting on your equity.
Total Asset Turnover = Net Sales - Average Total Assets
A company generates for each dollar of total assets it holds. Higher TAT suggests that the company is generating more sales relative to its investment in assets.
Accounts Receivables Turnover = Net Credit Sales / Average Accounts Receivable

Operating cash flow − cash CAPEX

Free cash flow measures a company's cash flow available for distribution to its investors or for future investments. A positive FCF indicates that a company is generating cash from its operations and co-invest in new projects, pay dividents, or reduce debt.

sections.heading: Unlevered and levered source variants

sections.heading: The valuation workflow and the source’s cost-of-equity expression
sections.body:
CAPM cost of equity
Risk-free rate + equity beta × (expected market return − risk-free rate)
Discounted Cash Flow (DCF)
DCF is used to estimate the intrinsic value of an investment or business by discounting future cash flows to their present value. It helps determine whether an investment opportunity is undervalued or overvalued.
DCF Usage
Historical financial analysis
The discount rate is the minimum rate of return acceptable to the investor. The absolute value of the discount rate depends on the definition of the discount rate. Namely, for cash flow after debt servicing, a simple discount rate is used, while for cash flow before debt servicing, a weighted average cost of capital (WACC) is used.
CAPEX and NEC forecast
Forecasting capital expenditures (capex) is an important part of the valuation modelling process, as it allows businesses to plan for and manage their investment in long-term assets.
Discount rate determination
The cost of equity is the expected rate of return that shareholders require to invest in a company’s common equity. In other words, it is the return that investors expect to receive on their investment in the form of dividends and capital gains. When conducting a valuation, the cost of equity is an important factor to consider as it reflects the investors' perception of risk associated with the company's future earnings. A higher risk perception means a higher cost of equity, and vice versa.
Discount Rate = risk free rate + investment beta (market rate - risk free rate)

sections.heading: Master budgets, static and flexible budgets, and rolling horizons
sections.body:
Master budget
The master budget coordinates all the financial projections in the organisation’s individual budgets in a single organisation-wide set of budgets
A master budget is a comprehensive expression of management’s operating and financial plans for a future time period (usually one year)
It embraces the impact of both operating decisions and financing decisions
Operating decisions centre on the use of scarce resources
Financing decisions centre on how to obtain the funds to acquire those resources
The term 'master' in 'master budget' refers to it being a comprehensive, organisation-wide set of budgets
Types of Budget
Master Budget
Overall financial and operational plan. Sub-budgets tied together
Summarises the financial projections of all the organisation’s individual budgets
Results in a set of related financial statements for a set time period, usually a year
= Operating + Financial budget
Activity based budgeting
Budgets for individual activity
Based on the principles of activity based costing (ABC) where cost drivers for activities are identified and then costed
Cash budget
Cash planning and Control. Aims to avoid idle cash and possible cash shortage
Part of the master budget that comprises capital budget, cash budget, budgeted balance sheet and budgeted statement of cash flows
Capital expenditure budget
Budgeting for long-term projects to be undertaken and capital to be acquired
Static (fixed) budget
Appropriate for departments whose work load does not have a direct current relationship to sales
A static budget is a budget that is based on one level of output
It is based on the level of output planned at the start of the budget period
It is not adjusted or altered after it is set
It is prepared at the start of the period when the actual output is known
Performance evaluation is difficult when actual activities differ from the planned level of activity
The master budget is an example of a static budget
Flexible (expense) budget
Dynamic and most commonly used
Flexible Budgets
A flexible budget shows revenues and expenses that should have occurred at the actual level of activity
A flexible budget is adjusted in accordance with changes in actual output
A flexible budget is prepared at the end of the period when the actual output is known
Flexible budget is used for both better planning and control
Improve performance evaluation
A key difference between a flexible budget and a static budget is the use of the actual output level in the flexible budget
Operating and Financial Budget
Operational budget deals with cost for merchandise and services produced. Financial budget examines expected asset liability and equity
Part of the master budget that comprises the budgeted profit statement

A 12-month rolling budget for Mar2018 to Feb2019 becomes a 12-month rolling budget for Apr2018 to Mar2018 and so on

sections.heading: Analysis prompts and common errors
sections.body:
Prompts for Understanding EBIT In Your Business
Compare EBIT to Revenue: What is the percentage or EBIT to your revenue? Is this percentage increasing or decreasing over time?
Compare EBIT to COGS: How does EBIT compare to the cost of goods sold (COGS)? Is the ratio increasing or decreasing?
EBIT Margin; Calculate your EBIT margin (EBIT divided by revenue)- How does this figure compare to industry benchmarks?
Year-on-year EBIT: Compare your EBIT on a year-on~year basis. Is it growing staying steady. or decreasing?
EBIT per Employee? How much EBIT does each employee generate? Is this figure increasing or decreasing?
EBIT by Product Line: Calculate EBIT for each product or service line. Which are the most and least profitable?
EBIT by Business Unit: Does your business have multiple units or departments, calculate the EBIT for each Which units are driving profitability?
Forecasting EBIT: Forecast EBIT for the next quarter. year, and three years. How do these projections compare to your strategic goals?
EBIT Sensitivity Analysis: Conduct a sensitivity analysis tor am. How do changes in sales volume, price. or costs affect EBIT?
Compare EBIT to Operating Cash Flow: How does EBIT compare to operating cash flow? Significant differences might indicate issues with working capital management.
EBIT and Capital Expendim: How does EBIT compare to your capital expenditure? High capital expenditure with low EBIT may indicate a need for efficiency improvements.
EBIT and Interest Expense: If you have significant debt, compare EBIT to your interest expense. Can your operational earnings cover interest payments?
EBIT and taxation: How does EBIT compareto your tax expense? This can provide insight into your effective tax rate.
EBIT and Dividends: Can your EBIT cover your dividend payments? If not, you might need to reevaluate your dividend policy.
EBIT and Investment: Compare EBIT to your investment income. This can show you how much of your profitability is driven by operations versus investments.
EBIT and Non-Operating Expenses: How does EBIT compare to hon-oparoting expenses? High non-operating expenses can distort your operational profitability.
EBIT and Depreciation: How does EBIT compare to depreciation? This can indicate whether your assets are generating sufficient profits.
EBIT and Amortisation If you have significant intangible assets, compare EBIT to amortisation this can help access the profitability at those assets.
Strategies to Avond Common EBIT Errors
Regularly update financial data: Outdated or incorrect data can lead to wrong EBIT calculations.
Understand the difference between operating and non-operating expenses: Oniy operating expenses should be subtracted In the EB" calculation.
Proper Classification of expenses: Be careful not to misclassify Indirect expenses as direct expenses.
Include all Income: Not just income from the main business activities. but also other relevant income sources
Don't mix up EBIT with EBITDA: EBITDA add back Depreciation and Amortisation to EBIT, they're not the same.
Professional financial advice: Consulting with a finance professional can help ensure the accuracy of
your EBIT calculation.

sections.heading: Strengths and weaknesses in the source
sections.body:
EBITDA strength and weakness
Strength
Relatively easy to calculate using information from a company's income statement and can be a simplified way to evaluate financial performance.
It can be a useful metric for comparing the performance of companies across industries and geographies, as it removes the impact of different tax rates, capital financing and capital structures in the comparison.
It can be used to evaluate a company's ability to generate cash flow from its operations, but only for companies with low CAPEX and slow growth.
It helps to identify trends in a company's operating performance over time, assuming a consistent formula is used across periods.
It helps exclude the impact of financing, capital investments and tax planning decisions from a company's operating performance.
It is often used as a valuation metric in mergers and acquisitions and can be useful as a benchmark for determining the value of a company.
Weakness
Not a standardised GAAP metric which allows for wide variation in how it is calculated.
Its use cases often imply that all income converts equally to cash, which is not accurate in practice.
Does not consider the required capital reinvestment.
Does not consider cash absorbed into working capital assets.
Could imply loan repayments will be made in priority which may not happen.
Doesn't reflect the quality of earnings which can lead to potential overstatement.
Poor measure of profitability due to differing accounting standards around the world.
Can't really compare acquisition multiples as it lacks industry specifics.
Can be misleading as it ignores real cash outflows like interest and taxes.
Can be manipulated through numerous accounting policies.

title: Accounts payable controls: responsibilities, checks and risks
summary: Compare payment, vendor, coding, matching and reconciliation controls in a structured matrix.

sections.heading: Control Overview
sections.body:
Accounts Payable
Control Overview
Control
Risk Mitigated
Segregation of Duties
Segregation of Duties (SOD) is a fundamental internal control principle that involves dividing key tasks and responsibilities among multiple individuals or departments.
Authorization - The approval or permission to perform a transaction. Recording— The documentation and recording of transactions. Custody- The physical control or handling of assets.
SOD ensures that no single individual has end-to-end control over a critical financial process, minimizing the potential for misuse or errors.
Preparer - Checker Control
The Preparer-Checker Control is an internal control designed to enhance accuracy and reliability in financial processes. The two individuals involved in a transaction are the "preparer" and the "checker."
The preparer initiates the transaction or prepares the documentation while the Checker independently reviews and verifies the accuracy of the work performed by the preparer.
This control is particularly effective in mitigating errors, preventing fraud, and ensuring that financial transactions meet the organization's standards.
Payment Authorisation
Establish a clear hierarchy for authorizing payments. Different individuals should be responsible for approving invoices and authorizing payments, with higher amounts requiring additional levels of approval.
Authorization— The person approving the payment should not have access to recording invoices. Recording— The person recording invoices and payments should not be authorized to approve payments.
Mitigating the risk of one individual being able to record and release payments without any checks and balances.
Vendor Verification and Approval
Vendor verification and approval are integral components of the accounts payable process, ensuring that organizations engage with legitimate and reputable suppliers.
The preparer initiates the vendor onboarding process, ensuring that all submitted vendor information is verified for accuracy and legitimacy. The approver independently reviews the vendor information
This control mechanism involves a systematic approach to validating vendors' identity, authenticity, and reliability before establishing business relationships or processing transactions.
Three-way Matching
Matching invoices with corresponding purchase orders and receiving reports (three-way match) is a critical step to ensure that the organization is billed accurately for goods or services received.
Match Purchase Order, Goods Receipt Note and invoice to ensure the accuracy of goods and services, quantity, unit and total price match across all three documents.
Three-way matching ensures accurate billing and prevents unauthorized or duplicate payments.
Accurate Coding and Classification of Expenses
This control ensures that each transaction is correctly identified, categorized, and recorded in the organization's accounting system.
The preparer codes and classifies expenses. The checker/approver reviews the coding as part of the approval process.
Implement controls to ensure that invoices are accurately coded and classified according to proper GL accounts, cost centers, or projects, facilitating accurate financial reporting and analysis.
Invoice and Payment Reconciliation
Invoice and payment reconciliation are critical internal controls. It involves comparing and verifying invoices with corresponding payments to ensure accuracy, completeness, and adherence to financial policies.
AP staff is often responsible for initiating the reconciliation process. A supervisor reviews the reconciliation conducted by the AP staff member. This adds an additional layer of verification.
Reconciliation ensures that the amounts on invoices match the actual payments made. This accuracy is fundamental for reliable financial reporting. It also helps prevent fraud and errors.
Duplicate Payment Prevention Control
Duplicate payments occur when the same invoice is paid more than once, leading to financial discrepancies. A Duplicate Payment Prevention control is essential for maintaining financial accuracy and preventing fraud.
Implement controls within the accounting system that can detect and flag potential duplicates as invoices are entered into the system, preventing erroneous payments before they occur.
Preventing duplicate payments ensures that financial records accurately reflect the accurate liabilities and expenses. It helps avoid payments otherwise being erroneously disbursed.
AP Sub-Ledger and General Ledger Reconciliation
The reconciliation between the Accounts Payable (AP) sub-ledger and the General Ledger is a critical internal control mechanism that ensures accuracy and consistency in financial reporting.
Conduct regular reconciliations between the AP sub-Ledger and the General Ledger. It should be done at least monthly. This includes verifying that the amounts, accounts, and transaction dates align.
By reconciling the AP sub-Ledger with the General Ledger, the organization can identify and correct any data entry errors, ensuring the accuracy and integrity issues between the sub-ledger and the general ledger.

sections.heading: Methods, adjustments and indicator labels
sections.body:
Methods
Comparable Uncontrolled Price (CUP) method
Compares the price charged in a controlled transaction to the price charged in a comparable uncontrolled transaction. Useful for commodity transactions. financial transactions. and transactions with very reliable internal comparables
Resale Price Method (RPM)
Assesses the gross margin with which a product purchased in the controlled transaction was resold in the uncontrolled transaction. Most appropriate for sales. marketing. and distribution transactions where internal compomics are available.
Cost Plus Method (CPM)
Test the gross markup on costs incurred by an enterprise during transactions with related parties. Suitable for manufacturing and service provision transactions where internal comparables are available.
Transactional Net Margin Method (TNMM)
Tests the net (operating) profit earned by a tested party of a controlled transaction. Often applied when a tested party can be identified no internal comparables are available and traditional methods are not reliable. TNMM is versatile and flexible and typically relies on external comparabies.
Transactional Profit Split Method (PSM)
Splits the profits to arrive at the result that would be achieved by independent parties in comparable transactions. Used for transactions where both parties make unique and valuable contributions (such as intangibles), and/or traditional methods are not appropriate due to the high integration of business operations.
Adjustments in transfer pricing
Comparability Adjustments
Changes that make the characteristics of uncontrolled transactions more comparable, enabling their use in transfer pricing method applications.
Year-End Adjustments
Changes that taxpayers can make at year-end to bring the results of their transactions Into the arm’s length range.
Primary Adjustments
Adjustments to a company's taxable profits made by a tax administration due to the application of the arm's length principle.These adjustments may lead to double taxation issues.
Corresponding Adjustments
Changes to the tax liability of a related party mode by the second tax jurisdiction corresponding to a primary adjustment. These adjustments are intended to resolve double taxation.
Secondary Adjustments
Constructive transactions introduced after a primary adjustment to align actual profit allocation with the primary adjustment. Can take the form of constructive dividends, equity contributions, or loans.

Operating Net Margin
Often used
Return on Assets
Rarely used
Berry Ratio
Relatively often used
Return on Total Costs
Often used
Return on capital employed
Rarely used

sections.heading: Culture, shared meanings and everyday ingredients
sections.body:
Culture Definition
Organisational culture: "the deeper level of basic assumptions and beliefs that are shared by members of an organisation, that operate unconsciously and define in a basic 'taken for granted' fashion on organisation's view of itself and its environment" (Schein, 1992)
Members of organisations are creating the organisation itself: organisations are socially constructed realities and, rather then being defined by their structures, rules and regulations, they are constructed as much in the heads and minds of their members and are strongly related to members' self-concepts and identity"
Culture is deep-seated and is likely to be resistant to change, but culture can be changed and is changing all the time (Bate, 1996).
"Organisations as cultures" (Morgan, 2006): in talking about culture, we are talking about a process of realty construction that allows people to see and understand particular events, actions, objects, utterances, or situations in distinctive ways
Culture has a cognitive (thinking), affective (feeling) and behavioural characteristics.
Requirement to examine how culture is created and sustained

sections.heading: Deal and Kennedy: risk and feedback
sections.body:
Model for corporate culture (Deal & Kennedy, 1982)
Tough-guy culture, macho culture: high risks and rapid feedback (software industry, investment banking, management consulting), focus on speed, competitive, conflictive / lack of cohesion
Work hard/play hard culture: low risk and quick feedback (sales organisations, office equipment, computers companies), persistence, working to recognize procedures, team-work / quantity v. quality
Bet-your-company culture: high risks and slow feedback (oil companies, aircraft manufacturers, capital goods), sense of deliberateness, ritualised decision meetings, top down, respect of authority and technical competence / unreactive
Process culture: low risk and slow feedback (banks, insurance companies, public organisations), technical perfection, process-oriented, seniority, positional power / unreactive

sections.heading: Occupational identity and communities of practice
sections.body:
Occupational identities
Occupational/professional identities: Lave and Wenger (1991) note that occupational identity formation is linked to a "situated learning" context where gradual acquisition of knowledge and skills occurs as novices to the occupational milieu learn via participation in everyday social practices within a social community"
Potential of tension between these identity foci, notably the mobilization of a broader occupational identity in resistance of managerial fiat: the collective norms and values of occupational identity can provide the basis for critiques of organisational change or legitimize alternative organisational narratives that compete with management attempts to create established narratives (McDonald et al. 2006)
Occupational communities are embedded in work practices, both formal and informal
The relationship between organisational and occupational identity is complex: organisations often provide the means for expression of occupational identity, the latter reinforces the former, leading to stronger organisational commitment
Occupational community members share a set of values born of common experience and histories, which underpin a sense of distinctiveness from non-members

title: Power and politics during organizational change

sections.heading: Power, relationships and political behavior
sections.body:
Power
Power is the capacity of individuals to overcome resistance on the part to others, to exert their will, and to produce results consistent with their interests and objectives.
The ability of individuals or groups to persuade, induce or coerce others into following certain courses of action.
Political behaviour in organisations consists of those activities that are not required as part of an individual’s formal role but that influence, or attempt to influence, the distribution of advantages and disadvantages within the organisation.
It is worth understanding both the sources of power and the indicators of power in an organisation.
Understanding stakeholder and coalitions and their likely responses to changes and proposed strategies is a useful tool in strategic analysis and evaluation.
Power means being able to influence the behaviour of others, sometimes in a direction which the person or group would not, otherwise, have chosen.
Power is a function of relationships. It is not something a person has regardless of what other people are thinking or doing.
Some people have more knowledge, expertise or resources than others do and, if these are scarce and desired, that peron or group will have more power than others.
This can be referred as the "elasticity of power".
Power to some extent is bestowed upon people by others; it is partly in the eyes of the beholder.
While knowledge and resources can give someone power, so can the belief by A that B can exercise power over them.
Handy (1993) refers to the « relativity of power » to describe a situation where one person or group perceives another to have power while the second person or group believes otherwise. Handy also notes that power is rarely one-sided.
Power is about the potential to influence as well as the actual use of influence.
Power can be seen as negative when it is characterized by a primitive, unsocialized need to have dominance over submissive others.
But power is part of organisational life.
Buchanan's research (2008) shows that the experience of politics seems to be frequent, visible and sometimes painful.
Five behaviours occur frequently : building a network of useful contacts, using key players to support initiatives, making friends with power brokers, bending the rules to fit the situation, and self-promotion.

sections.heading: How change redistributes influence
sections.body:
Change and the use of power
Organisational life is full of occasions when people try to influence how others perceive the world around them.
Organisations facing conditions of change are, in many respects, at their most vulnerable to the political actions of those who stand to gain from the change as well as those who stand to lose.
Any change brings about new organisational uncertainties that will "offer" occasions for organisational actors to position themselves, to promote their views and to gain power.
Some changes are less problematic than others. Radical change is more likely to bring the greatest conditions of fear and uncertainty.
Even so, small-scale, incremental change can upset the balance of power through small but significant redistribution of resources or changes in structure that make the skills or experience of some people more desirable than others.
Some types of change challenge the values and beliefs of some of the people involved, or their own goals, and induce an internal state of conflict that, in turn, raises their resistance to change.
They will mobilize their resources to pursue strategies that can be
Defensive or pro-active
Individual or collective
These strategies can take different directions
Alliance
Opposition
Negotiation
In a change process, there is generally a "change agent" who has the responsibility for planning, implementation and outcome of strategic change.
Power plays a role in influencing the success of strategic implementation but the relationships between power and success is complex.
Different types of power are enacted in different ways and the effects of power are mediated by the different implementation processes used.
Change is about the capacity to influence and lead, and recognizes other people’s needs to achieve their own goals as well as those of the organisations.

sections.heading: Intrinsic motivation: autonomy, mastery and purpose

Motivating Changes
Different approaches to motivation
Intrinsic: satisfaction and pleasure linked to the task/job.
Extrinsic: incentives and rewards outside of an individual.
Daniel Pink (2011) in his book "Drive" argues that extrinsic motivation is not as potent as managers might think. For him, intrinsic motivation is the main driver for individuals and suggest to consider three main factors
Autonomy: people like to be self-directed with a high degree of freedom to decide the direction, methods and circumstances of their work. In a situation of change, managers should then create decision-making opportunities, avoid micromanagement and encourage ownership.
Mastery: people like to do things well and to get better at doing things they value, so opportunities to grow, develop and excel at their work are motivating. Managers should encourage individuals and teams to improve their skills and knowledge and to support their growth.
Purpose: people like to feel their work has meaning and value and they will choose to invest in activities they consider worthwhile. Managers should ensure that the purpose of change is communicated clearly and that people understand the purpose and the rationale for change, and that they know how they will contribute towards the purpose of the change.

sections.heading: Origins, participation and systems thinking
sections.body:
Organisation Development
A process that applies behavioural science knowledge and practices to help organizations build the capacity to change an achieve greater effectiveness (…) OD differs from other planned change efforts, such as project management, because the focus is on building the organization’s ability to assess its current functioning and to achieve its goals.
It is a soft system for change which emphasizes not just the content and control of change but also the process by which change comes about
OD developed primarily in the USA out of a number of different schools of thought and practice that have included applied behavioural sciences, sociology, systems thinking, and psychotherapy.
Kurt Lewin’s work on group dynamics, action research and the consultant-client dynamic, form the early foundations of OD.
American psychologists and behaviourists working in the late 1940s and 1950s found that the application of participative methods to small groups led to attitude change, higher performance and greater commitment.
Abraham Maslow argued for the inherent potential of individuals to pursue ‘self actualisation’, which was more likely to be achieved under conditions of openness and personal recognition.
Organization theorists like Chris Argyris and Rensis Likert advocated organization-wide participation as a means of motivating individuals and hence achieving greater performance.
In the 1960s, the term ‘organization development’ was introduced as an overarching umbrella for managing and developing the behavioural aspects of people in organizations.
The OD approach to change is, above all, an approach that cares about people and which believes that people at all levels throughout an organization are, individually and collectively, both the drivers and the engines of change.
Groups interact and overlap to form larger organizational systems that, in their turn, influence an organization’s capacity to learn and change.
OD acknowledges the systemic nature of organizational life and that changes in one part of the organization will impact on operations in another part.
Any organization is a balance of forces built up and refined over a period of time : proposed change will inevitably change this balance and will almost certainly encounter resistance.
Besides, it is based on a number of assumptions regarding people in groups
People are in general social beings - they will form formal and informal groups
Consequently the work group becomes very important in any attempt at change

sections.heading: Common features of organization development
sections.body:
Common features
OD work is based upon robust diagnosis that uses real data from organizational, behavioral and psychological sources. OD is based on the application and transfer of behavioural science knowledge and practice (such as leadership, group dynamics and work design), and is distinguished by its ability to transfer such knowledge and skill so that the system is capable of carrying out more planned change in the future.
OD work is planned and systemic in its focus and takes account of the whole organization. OD applies to changes in the strategy, structure, and/or processes of an entire system, such as an organisation, a single plant of a multi-plant firm, a department or work group, or individual role or job.
OD is concerned with managing planned change, in a flexible manner that can be revised as new information is gathered.
OD involves both the creation and the subsequent reinforcement. of change by institutionalizing change.
OD is orientated to improving organizational effectiveness by:
Helping members of the organization to gain the skills and knowledge necessary to solve problems by involving them in the change process, and;
Promoting high performance including financial returns, high quality products and services, high productivity, continuous improvement and a high quality of working life.

Human Resource
Key Findings
Design employee experiences by segmenting and understanding the work lives of your people. Design thinking takes into account how people already work, make decisions and otherwise organize their day and effort – and uses that knowledge to build specific HR-driven tools to help employees meet goals, improve skills, collaborate and feel more engaged.
Use HR technology to help improve people's productivity and experience at work. HR-driven technology has the potential to do much more than automate existing practices. High-impact HR organizations find opportunities to use technology to improve productivity, feedback, and alignment among teams throughout the company.
Lead the company's digital transformation. As many companies struggle to understand what the digital revolution means for their businesses, HR is uniquely specifically positioned to lead rather than follow. Organizational structure, reward systems and incentives – all under the purview of HR – are critical pieces for businesses in reaching the digital future.
Understand and support agile and team-centric organizational models. Traditional hierarchies no longer represent the way that most work really gets done. High-impact HR organizations offer collaborative solutions to help constantly shifting team structures with issues such as goal management, performance management, coaching, check-ins, and development.
Work with leadership to shape a culture of trust, inclusion, purpose, and accountability. High-impact HR organizations don't just focus on compliance and control – the ‘hard issues’. By focusing on culture, high-performance HR teams are able to address multiple entry points for ‘soft issues’.
Design the HR function to operate as a network of teams, breaking down silos within the HR function and with the rest of the business. While specialization in issues like recruiting, learning, compensation and other key functions is important, almost all problems today are multi-disciplinary. High impact HR teams operate as agile consulting groups, bringing together all the disciplines into action when a problem emerges.
Regenerate, professionalize, and continuously develop your HR professionals. Demand the same level of growth and innovation as you would from other functions of the business and give your people lots of opportunities for developmental assignments, external education, research, and visits to peer

title: Emotions at work: change, emotional labour and awareness
