title: Pension funds: a historical 100-fund ranking and its limits
summary: Explore all 100 entries from the supplied pension infographic as a dated historical reference, with source credits, reporting exceptions and graphic annotations.

sections.heading: Read the historical ranking and reporting notes
sections.body: Top 100 Largest Pension Funds

sections.heading: Graphic, publisher and data source
sections.body:
The supplied infographic is Visual Capitalist’s “Ranked: The World’s 100 Biggest Pension Funds,” published 24 November 2022. Research/writing: Jenna Ross. Design: Sam Parker. The image credits Thinking Ahead Institute and Pensions & Investments (September 2022). The complete rank, fund, market and rounded-asset data are reconstructed below and checked against the publisher’s structured table.
The original legend uses circle size for total assets, a number for global rank and rings for ranks 1–100, with the largest funds on inner rings. Logos, country colors and flags identify entries; they are not investment-quality ratings. The table replaces the oversized visual while preserving its data and source record.

sections.heading: Reporting cutoffs and source exceptions
sections.body:
The default cutoffs in the image are 30 September 2021 for US funds and 31 December 2021 for non-US funds. Exceptions dated 31 March 2022: Canada Pension, Pension Fund Association in Japan, BT Group in the UK and Organization for Workers in Japan.
The image marks estimates for National Social Security in China, Public Institute for Social Security in Kuwait, Boeing, Employees’ Provident in India, AT&T, General Motors, Employees’ Pension Fund in India, Ford, Wells Fargo, Verizon, J.P. Morgan Chase and Social Insurance Funds in Vietnam.
Other cutoffs: 1 January 2022 for Russia’s National Wealth Fund; 30 June 2021 for AustralianSuper, Aware Super, QSuper, UniSuper and Sunsuper; 31 March 2021 for Canada’s Public Service Pension Plan and the UK’s Universities Superannuation and Electricity Supply Pension; 31 January 2022 for Germany’s Bayerische Versorgungskammer.
The graphic predates the 2022 QSuper/Sunsuper merger and displays both separately. It says Royal Bank of Scotland Group and Lloyds Banking Group amounts are global group figures. These footnotes belong to the historical source, not a refreshed dataset.

sections.heading: Country annotations retained from the graphic
sections.body:
Japan: the graphic describes GPIF as a defined-benefit plan for public-sector employees and says it had led the ranking since 2002. United States: it describes nearly half the top 100 as US funds, totaling more than $6 trillion. These are historical source descriptions, not independently updated findings.
India: the graphic describes Employees’ Provident contributions totaling 26.16% of earnings, split 13% employer, 12% employee and 1.16% government. This is preserved as a dated chart claim, not current contribution guidance.
China: the graphic describes National Social Security as a top-up fund financed through government, lottery ticket sales and state-owned enterprises, with a Yahoo Finance September 2020 attribution. Russia: it reports a $16 billion National Wealth Fund withdrawal to help cover the 2022 budget deficit, citing Reuters October 2022.
Norway: the chart says its Government Pension Fund held investments in more than 9,000 companies across 70 countries and was the largest single owner in world stock markets. UK: it describes the largest listed funds as company plans or industry pools. Both statements are retained as historical chart annotations.
Sweden: the graphic describes the AP funds as part of the national pension system for people who have worked and paid taxes in the country. Canada: it describes Healthcare of Ontario as a defined-benefit healthcare-workers’ plan based on employment earnings and years of contribution. These source summaries simplify scheme details and are not eligibility or benefit rules.

sources.title: Visual Capitalist: the world’s 100 biggest pension funds, published November 2022

title: Economic foundations: scarcity, work and choices
summary: Connect scarce resources, economic indicators, employment and choices over time.

sections.heading: Scarcity and the indicators to watch
sections.body:
Concept clarified
Scarcity means choices compete for limited resources. The jigsaw is a coordination metaphor, not evidence that markets always reach a desirable result. Read growth, inflation, unemployment and wages together: a growing total can coexist with falling purchasing power for some households.
Economics
Basic
The scarcity and consumption of resources
Economy is like a jigsaw puzzle with billion pieces that miraculously assembles itself
Main economic indicators
Inflation, growth, unemployment, wages

sections.heading: Jobs, migration and local demand
sections.body:
Concept clarified
Unemployment and underemployment describe different labour-market problems. Migration can increase demand for services and also changes labour supply, skills and capacity; the net result depends on the place, period and institutions. The source gives no dataset for its one-way claim.
Unemployment ≠ Underemployment
More immigrants = more demand for local services

sections.heading: Partnerships and decisions under uncertainty
sections.body:
Concept clarified
Public-private partnership is a delivery/financing arrangement; it is different from purchasing power parity, which shares the initials PPP. Subjective expected utility weights possible outcomes by the decision maker’s beliefs and utilities, rather than simply estimating an investment return.
Public-private partnership (PPP)
Subjective Expected Utility (SEU)
Each individual calculates the likelihood of return on investment

sections.heading: Receiving value sooner or later
sections.body:
Concept clarified
Time discounting describes preferences over timing. A financial discount rate also incorporates assumptions about risk and financing; do not substitute a psychological preference for an audited valuation model.
Time discounting
The current relative valuation placed on receiving a good at an earlier date compared with receiving it at a later date
Cycle

title: Measuring an economy: GDP, inequality and purchasing power
summary: Distinguish output, price-level comparisons, investment and broader measures of progress.

sections.heading: Gini: name the distribution
sections.body:
Concept clarified
A Gini coefficient summarizes inequality in a specified distribution. Income and wealth Ginis are different measures; specify population, date and whether income is before or after taxes and transfers. One number does not identify the causes of inequality.
Gini coefficient
A measure of statistical dispersion intended to represent the income or wealth distribution of a nation's residents, and is the most commonly used measure of inequality

sections.heading: Money identities and the investment ratio
sections.body:
Concept clarified
The chain “GDP = MV = PT = CV” is not a valid general identity. Nominal GDP counts final domestic production; a transactions aggregate can include transactions outside GDP. Credit outstanding is a stock and cannot simply replace money in an identity using the same velocity.
With consistently defined aggregates, MV = PY is a nominal-income identity, where Y is real output and P its price level. An identity alone does not prove that money growth causes proportional inflation. GFCF divided by GDP is an investment share when period, currency and valuation are consistent.
GDP = MV = PT = CV
M = Money - average amount of money in circulation in the community during the year
V = Velocity - average rate of turnover of money
P = Price level - weighted average of all prices
T = Trade - volume of trade
C = Total credit market debt
Investment ratio
Gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) / gross domestic product (GDP)

sections.heading: Quantity equation versus Fisher interest relationship
sections.body:
Concept clarified
The source calls a quantity equation the “Fisher identity” and equates transaction volume with GDP. Keep the quantity relationship separate from the Fisher relationship between nominal interest, real interest and expected inflation; the approximate rate relation is i ≈ r + expected inflation, not the money-times-velocity equation.
Fisher identity
Money in circulation x velocity = average transaction price x volume of transaction (GDP)

sections.heading: Progress measures and purchasing power parity
sections.body:
Concept clarified
GPI supplements or adjusts conventional output accounting; the source supplies no specification or data series. Purchasing power parity compares currencies using the prices of a comparable basket. A PPP conversion differs from a market exchange rate; choose the conversion appropriate to the comparison.
Genuine progress indicator (GPI)
Alternative view on economic health
Purchasing power parity (PPP)
Real economic value under real-world exchange rate that is adjusted GDP

title: Money and banking: policy tools, crises and distribution
summary: Follow the differences between creating money, lending liquidity, rescuing institutions and changing incentives.

sections.heading: Seigniorage and corrective taxation
sections.body:
Concept clarified
Seigniorage concerns the economic benefit from issuing money; “note versus face value” omits production cost, interest and institutional accounting. Pigouvian taxation targets an external cost. A sugar or tobacco tax is not automatically set equal to an accurately measured marginal harm.
Seigniorage
Profit made by the government from the difference between note and face value
Pigouvian taxes
Taxes match the cost of harm done (e.g. sugar or tobacco)

sections.heading: Shadow banking, lender of last resort and QE
sections.body:
Concept clarified
Non-bank financial intermediation can create bank-like credit and liquidity risks without being identical to regulated deposit banking. Emergency lending supplies liquidity under particular eligibility, collateral and risk conditions; it does not automatically repair insolvency.
QE is central-bank asset purchasing that changes balance sheets and financial conditions. It is more specific than “introducing new money.” Negative policy rates do not mean every household pays a negative rate on every deposit.
Shadow banking: non-bank financial institutions that operate like banks
Central banks could replace lost deposits by providing official loans to a bank experiencing a run
Quantitative easing
The introduction of new money into the money supplied by a central bank
Negative interest rate policy
To encourage spending by having to pay to deposit money in the bank

sections.heading: A bailout is not simply a new creditor
sections.body:
Concept clarified
A bailout supplies support to an institution or sector in distress; it can involve loans, guarantees, capital or other measures. Refinancing or transferring a debt to a new creditor is not by itself a bailout.
Bailout
Taking over a position and the debtor owes another creditor

sections.heading: Say and Gresham: propositions with conditions
sections.body:
Concept clarified
Say’s law is a historical proposition about production, income and demand, not a guarantee that each product will sell. Gresham’s mechanism concerns competing monies under a constrained exchange valuation; avoid applying “bad drives out good” to every market.
Say’s law
Supply creates its own demand, meaning production generates the income needed to purchase goods.
Gresham’s law
"Bad money drives out good money," meaning people will hoard valuable currency and spend less valuable currency.

sections.heading: The Triffin dilemma
sections.body:
Concept clarified
A reserve-currency issuer can face tension between domestic objectives and international demand for reserve assets. This is a structural dilemma, not a dated exchange-rate forecast.
Triffin dilemma
The conflict between a country's short-term economic interests and its long-term role as a global reserve currency provider.

sections.heading: Who receives new money first?
sections.body:
Concept clarified
The Cantillon effect names distributional effects associated with how money enters an economy. The incidence depends on transmission channels and behaviour; proximity to a central bank is not a sufficient empirical measure.
Cantillon effect
Unequal distribution of wealth and income resulting from changes in the money supply, benefiting those closest to the source of money.

sections.heading: Money, regulation and the business cycle
sections.body:
Concept clarified
The source’s “government law,” “money law” and “banking law” labels are topic headings, not named universal laws. They cover public authority, currency, interest rates, bank regulation, saving and the possible short-run real effects of money.
Public ownership does not guarantee bank stability. Saving and spending are connected through income and investment rather than an unchanging ideal balance. Business fluctuations need not repeat at fixed intervals. The fused interest-rate sentence is preserved below with the rest of the source wording.
Government law
Rules and regulations that define the structure, powers, and functions of government institutions and their relationship with citizens.
Money law
Governs the creation, regulation, and use of money within an economy, including currency, banking, and financial transactions.
Money prices law
The value of money and prices are influenced by the supply and demand for goods, services, and currency.
Interest rates lawThe cost of borrowing money (interest rates) is influenced by factors like inflation, central bank policies, and economic conditions.
Banking law
Governs the operations, regulations, and practices of banks, including lending, deposits, and financial services.
Government-controlled banking law
Regulates banks that are owned or heavily influenced by the government, aiming to stabilise the economy and ensure financial security.
Spending vs. saving law
Individuals or economies must balance expenditure and savings to maintain financial stability and long-term growth.
Non-Neutrality of money law
Changes in the money supply can affect real economic variables, such as output and employment, in the short run.
Business cycles and depression law
Economies experience periodic fluctuations, with booms followed by recessions or depressions due to factors like investment and consumption changes.

title: Economic cycles: mechanisms, hypotheses and misleading clocks
summary: Compare credit, investment, innovation and confidence explanations without treating suggested periods as predictions.

sections.heading: Named cycles and their limits
sections.body:
Concept clarified
Kondratieff, Kuznets, Juglar and Kitchin refer to proposed fluctuations at different horizons. The quoted periods are historical labels, not reliable timers. The 18-year property claim is attributed in the notes to Phillip J. Anderson without a citation; no forecast is established. “Humanity” scenarios are an unattributed taxonomy, not measured business-cycle evidence.
Kondratieff’s long wave
Hypothesised cycle-like phenomena in the modern world economy
Kuznets swing
Medium-range economic wave with a period of 15–25 years
Juglar cycle
Fixed investment cycle of 7 to 11 years
Kitchin cycle
Short business cycle of about 40 months
Humanity
Recurrent collapse, plateau, extinction, takeoff
18-year real-estate cycle
Phillip J. Anderson - 14 years and 4 years down

sections.heading: Ten proposed sources of fluctuations
sections.body:
Concept clarified
Despite its “Microeconomy” heading, this source section discusses economy-wide fluctuations: weather, expectations, sentiment, innovation, saving/investment, construction, excess production, credit, income distribution and profits. These are competing or interacting mechanisms. Weather shocks are not proof of a deterministic sunspot cycle; the final quotation has no source attribution.
Microeconomy
The weather
Weather patterns and sunspots are held to affect agricultural prices and, thereby, the broader economy.
Uncertainty
The business community tends to misjudge future demand and overproduce or underproduce as a result. The need to adjust output to actual demand then sets off the cycle.
The emotional factor in business decisions
Mood swings within the business community between excessive optimism and excessive pessimism are thought responsible for the booms and busts of investment.
Innovation, promotion, progress
This theory states that innovations and waves of innovations cause changes in both the supply and demand for products to which the economy must adjust.
The process of saving and investments
One version of this theory blames the business cycle on a scarcity of capital, while another attributes it to over-saving.
Construction work
This theory contends that booms and depressions originate in the construction industry and spread out to the rest of the economy.
General overproduction
Investment by the business community sets off a period of prosperity, but then carries on for too long until there is excess production that can’t be sold. At that point, investment is reduced, resulting in depression.
Banking operations
Credit expansion causes the boom, but the boom goes into reverse when credit ceases to expand.
Production and the flow of money incomes
Production expands faster than wages, eventually leading to unsold goods, falling prices and depression.
The role played by profit-making
“The distinguishing characteristic of these theories is that they represent the alternatives of prosperity and depression as arising from profit-making itself”

sections.heading: Debt deflation and a mixed list of outcomes
sections.body:
Concept clarified
The coherent debt-deflation chain is: distress selling, repayment and contracting credit, falling prices, heavier real debt burdens, weaker balance sheets and output, then worsening confidence. It is a feedback mechanism rather than an inevitable sequence.
The remaining notes mix bear markets, worker shortages, trading descriptions and political labels. Worker shortages do not follow necessarily from debt deflation; recession does not imply nationalisation or communism. “Vulnerable and buyable” has no valuation method or decision rule.
Deflationary
Debt liquidation leads to distress selling
Contraction of deposit currency, bank loans paid off, circulation slowed down
Fall in level prices = swelling of the dollar
Fall in net worth of business = increase bankruptcies
Fall in profit - Reduction in output = unemployment
Pessimism and loss of confidence
Hoarding and slowing down still more the velocity of circulation
Prolonged bear market
Shortage of workers
Higher employment cost
Prices are sold aggressively
Uncertainty and choppy activity
Vulnerable and buyable
Recession
Depression
Nationalisation
Communism

title: Economic schools and thinkers: a comparative reading map
summary: Separate schools of explanation from mnemonic labels and incomplete historical attributions.

sections.heading: An unattributed philosophical grouping
sections.body:
Concept clarified
The optimistic/pessimistic and definite/indefinite pairings are preserved as a supplied classification. No author, rationale or primary text is given for assigning these philosophers to the four cells; this is not presented as an established history-of-philosophy taxonomy.
Class
Definite optimistic
Hegel & Marx
Indefinite optimistic
Nozick & Rawls
Pessimistic definite
Plato & Aristotle
Pessimistic indefinite
Epicurus & Lucretius

sections.heading: Nine schools at a glance
sections.body:
Classical
Emphasizes the role of free markets and the self-regulating nature of economic systems.
Neoclassical
Centers on individual choice and the mathematical modeling of market behavior.
Marxist
Economic development is driven by material conditions and social relations.
Developmentalist
Concentrates on the economic strategies of developing countries and how they can achieve sustained growth.
Austrian
Stresses the importance of individual action and the limitations of government intervention.
Schumpeterian
Highlights the role of innovation and entrepreneurship in driving economic growth and transformation.
Keynesian
Advocates for government intervention to stabilize economies and smooth out business cycles.
Institutionalist
Examines the role of institutions and social norms in shaping economic outcomes and behavior.
Behaviourist
Focuses on the psychological and cognitive aspects of economic decision-making and challenges the assumption of perfect rationality in traditional economic models.

sections.heading: Thinkers: correct the spelling and the attribution
sections.body:
Concept clarified
Read “Thomas Robert Maithus” as Thomas Robert Malthus and “Frederick Hoyak” as Friedrich Hayek. These are editorial identification corrections. The Manifesto was coauthored by Marx and Engels. Nash is central to equilibrium theory, but the prisoner’s dilemma was not originated by Nash. Slogans such as “show me the money” are memory aids, not book titles or quotations. The source’s “Behaviourist” school description is closer to behavioural economics than to the distinct psychology school of behaviourism.
Theories
The wealth of nations
Adam Smith
The dismal outlook by dismal science
Thomas Robert Maithus
The communist manifesto
Karl Marx
Keynesian; government spending on rescue
John Maynard Keynes
The wonders of creative destruction
Joseph Schumpeter
Set my market free
Frederick Hoyak
Prisoner’s dilemma
John Nash
Long-term growth as people, capital, and technology
Robert Solow
Show me the money
Milton Friedman

title: Political and economic systems: power, ownership and ideology
summary: Organize terms by what they describe, rather than treating every label as a form of government.

sections.heading: Who holds power?
sections.body:
Government
Plutocracy
A form of government or society ruled or controlled by the wealthy.
Oligarchy
A government or organization controlled by a small group of people, often from a specific class or group.
Democracy
A system of government where power is vested in the people, typically through elected representatives.
Meritocracy
A system in which advancement and leadership are based on individual ability and talent rather than on wealth or social class.
Aristocracy
A form of government or social structure in which power is held by the nobility

sections.heading: Ownership and concentrations of influence
sections.body:
Capitalism
An economic system characterized by private ownership of the means of production and the pursuit of profit.
Kleptocracy
A government or state in which those in power exploit national resources and steal; rule by corrupt leaders.
Corporatocracy
A society or system where corporate interests and corporations have significant control over government policy and decision-making.

sections.heading: Economic systems and political traditions
sections.body:
Socialism
An economic and political system where the means of production are owned and controlled by the state or public.
Communism
A classless, stateless society where all property and resources are communally owned.
Marxism / Neo Marxism
A theory developed by Karl Marx, advocating for a classless society through the abolition of capitalism and the establishment of socialism.
Fascism
A far-right, authoritarian political ideology that emphasizes nationalism, dictatorial power, and the suppression of opposition.
Nationalism
A political ideology that emphasizes the interests, culture, and value of one's nation, often above those of other nations.
Leninism
A form of Marxism developed by Vladimir Lenin that advocates for the establishment of a vanguard party to lead the proletarian revolution and establish a dictatorship of the proletariat.
Maoism
A form of Marxism-Leninism developed by Mao Zedong, emphasizing the role of the peasantry in revolution and the importance of continuous class struggle.
Anarchism
A political philosophy that advocates for a stateless society where individuals govern themselves without hierarchical authority.
Liberalism
A political and economic philosophy emphasizing individual freedoms, democracy, and the protection of civil liberties.

sections.heading: Philosophy, favouritism and historical repression
sections.body:
Nihilism
A philosophical belief that life is meaningless and rejects all religious and moral principles.
Cronyism
Favoritism shown to close friends or associates, especially in political appointments or business dealings.
Nepotism
Favoritism granted to relatives in various fields, such as employment, business, or politics.
McCarthyism
A period of intense anti-communist suspicion in the United States during the early 1950s, characterized by accusations and investigations.
Contractarianism
Individuals make the right choices under a hypothetical social contract

sections.heading: Keep the categories distinct
sections.body:
Capitalism and socialism concern ownership and coordination; democracy and oligarchy concern the distribution of political power. An economy can combine institutions from several categories. Meritocracy is an ideal of selection and advancement, not a complete constitution.
The concise definitions are study prompts. Socialism includes traditions beyond state ownership; communism’s theoretical end state differs from states historically ruled by communist parties. Nihilism is a family of philosophical positions, not one universal denial of every value. Contractarianism concerns justification through agreement, not a guarantee that hypothetical choices are always right. Cronyism and nepotism describe practices; McCarthyism names a historical campaign and its associated methods.

title: Trade, development and inequality
summary: Connect cross-border exchange, urban change and competing explanations of unequal outcomes.

sections.heading: Trade barriers
sections.body:
Concept clarified
Tariffs, quotas and subsidies change prices and incentives in different ways. Identify the affected goods, trading partners and policy objective before calling a measure a barrier or judging its distributional effects.
External factors
Barriers to trade, tariffs, quotas, subsidies

sections.heading: Thirteen processes of social and economic change
sections.body:
Socioeconomics
Globalisation
The process by which businesses, cultures, and societies become integrated and interdependent on a global scale. This includes the flow of goods, services, information, and people across borders. It’s driven by advancements in technology, transportation, and communication.
Glocalisation
The adaptation of global business practices and products to fit local cultures and preferences. It combines global and local considerations to tailor offerings to specific markets.
Urbanisation
The movement of populations from rural to urban areas, leading to the growth of cities and towns. This process is associated with economic development, industrialization, and changes in lifestyle.
Industrialization
The transformation from an agrarian society to one based on the manufacturing of goods and services. This involves the development of industries and factories, leading to increased production and economic growth.
Localisation
The emphasis on local production, consumption, and decision-making to preserve local identity and reduce dependency on global networks. It often contrasts with globalization by focusing on strengthening local economies and cultures.
Nationalisation
The transfer of private sector assets into public ownership. Governments take control of industries or resources to ensure their management serves the public interest.
Regionalisation
The division or organization of a country or area into smaller regions for administrative, economic, or cultural purposes. It also refers to the cooperation between neighboring regions or countries to promote economic integration and development.
Liberalisation
The process of reducing government regulations and restrictions in the economy to encourage free-market activity. It often involves the deregulation of industries, reduction of tariffs, and opening up to foreign investment.
Imperialism
The policy or practice of extending a country's power and influence through colonization, military force, or other means. It often involves the domination and exploitation of weaker territories.
Colonialism
A form of imperialism where a country establishes settlements and exerts control over the political and economic systems of another territory. It typically involves the exploitation of resources and indigenous populations.
Expansionism
The policy of territorial or economic expansion by a nation. It involves the acquisition of new lands or markets through diplomacy, military conquest, or other means.
Isolationism
A national policy of avoiding political or economic entanglements with other countries. It focuses on self-reliance and non-intervention in international affairs.
Feudalism
A medieval European social system where land was owned by lords who allowed peasants to live on it in return for labor or military service. It structured society around relationships derived from the holding of land in exchange for service or labor.

sections.heading: Gravity and factor endowments
sections.body:
Concept clarified
The gravity model relates bilateral trade to economic size and trade frictions, often proxied partly by distance. Heckscher–Ohlin emphasizes relative factor abundance under model assumptions; neither statement predicts each country’s exports without qualification.
Laws
Gravity model
Predicts trade flow between two countries based on their economic sizes and the distance between them.
Heckscher-Ohlin model
Countries export goods requiring abundant resources and import goods needing scarce resources.

sections.heading: The Leontief paradox
sections.body:
Concept clarified
The historical finding challenged a simple factor-endowment prediction for US trade under the measurement and assumptions used. It is a test of a model in a setting, not proof that endowments never matter.
Leontief paradox
Exported labor-intensive goods contradicting the Heckscher-Ohlin model.

sections.heading: Demand similarity, inequality and mercantilism
sections.body:
Concept clarified
Linder emphasizes overlapping demand as a possible trade explanation. The Kuznets inequality hypothesis is distinct from the Kuznets cycle. Piketty’s r > g relationship is a mechanism to examine, not a sufficient law of inevitable inequality: taxation, saving, institutions and shocks also matter. Mercantilism describes an orientation to trade and state power; a trade surplus alone is not a complete welfare measure.
Linder hypothesis
Countries with similar demand patterns are more likely to trade with each other.
Kuznets hypothesis
As an economy develops, income inequality first increases and then decreases over time.
Piketty’s r > g hypothesis
Return on capital (r) exceeds economic growth (g), wealth inequality increases.
Mercantilism & neomercantilism
Maximising exports and minimising imports to accumulate wealth.

sections.heading: Equality is a question to specify
sections.body:
Concept clarified
“Equality and inequality law” names a subject, not an established equation. Specify equality of what—income, wealth, opportunity, rights or outcomes—before choosing a measure or evaluating a policy.
Equality and inequality law
The balance or imbalance in the distribution of resources, rights, and opportunities within a society.

sections.heading: A historical globalization quotation
sections.body:
Editorial clarification
The Glyn and Sutcliffe quotation is dated 1992 in the notes. It concerns the authors’ historical comparison; no complete publication/page is supplied. Preserve it as a dated research prompt rather than current evidence of globalization’s level.
Globalisation
In short, the world economy is considerably more globalised than 50 years ago; but much less so than is theoretically possible. The widespread view that the present degree of globalisation is in some way new and unprecedented is, therefore, false. (Glyn and Sutcliffe, 1992)

title: Banking institutions and economic history: a dated reading guide
summary: Put Basel standards, monetary arrangements and crisis episodes in their historical context.

sections.heading: The Opium Wars and Hong Kong
sections.body:
Incomplete historical prompt
The two-line note is an incomplete historical prompt. Trade, coercion and imperial power require a fuller account than “a trade war”; the document supplies no dates, treaty text or citation. The strategic-port statement is retained without pretending this is a complete causal history.
Opium war
Due to the trade war, HK was a strategic port

sections.heading: Basel standards and European supervision
sections.body:
Concept clarified
1974 refers to the Basel Committee’s establishment, whereas Basel I was released in 1988. Basel II’s three pillars and Basel III’s post-crisis reforms belong to successive frameworks. The “130 biggest banks” note is historical, not a current count of ECB-supervised institutions.
Notable History
European central bank (ECB) directly supervised eurozone 130 biggest banks
Basel I
The BCBS was founded in 1974 as an international forum where members could cooperate on banking supervision matters.
Basel II
Minimum capital requirements, regulatory supervision and market discipline
Basel III
Art of the continuous effort to enhance the banking regulatory framework. It builds on the Basel I and Basel II documents, and seeks to improve the banking sector's ability to deal with financial stress, improve risk management, and strengthen the banks’ transparency.

sections.heading: A timeline of policy responses and institutions
sections.body:
Historical notes; context incomplete
The Powell memorandum, Roosevelt’s programmes, Hamilton’s debt plan, Bretton Woods and LTCM are distinct historical topics, not one causal sequence. The source gives only memory prompts; its LTCM entry identifies the 1998 crisis. Hamilton’s funding and assumption proposals should not collapse all federal and state obligations into one category. No missing quotations or programme details have been invented.
The Powell memo
A call-to-arms for USA corporations
Franklin D. Roosevelt (FDR)
Promoting programs to combat the economic crisis besetting the USA
Hamilton's financial plan
The federal government should pay off all Confederation (state) debts at full value
Bretton Woods system
Required a currency peg to the U.S. dollar which was in turn pegged to the price of gold.
Long Term Capital Management (LTCM)
Hedge fund blew up in 1998

title: Production, prices and the limits of economic “laws”
summary: Read output, costs, incentives and coordination as conditional relationships rather than slogans.

sections.heading: The Laffer curve does not identify a tax rate
sections.body:
Concept clarified
The curve proposes a relationship between a tax rate and receipts under particular behavioural assumptions. It does not establish the revenue-maximizing rate for a real tax base without evidence.
Laffer curve
Theoretical relationship between rates of taxation and the resulting levels of the government's tax revenue

sections.heading: Substitution is not a named universal law
sections.body:
Concept clarified
The “law of replacement” is an unattributed label. Scarcity or higher relative prices can encourage substitution, but technical constraints, switching costs and preferences can prevent it. No missing theorem is inferred.
Law of replacement
Resources or goods will be replaced or substituted when they become scarce or too expensive.

sections.heading: Trade-offs and the Lindy heuristic
sections.body:
Concept clarified
The free-lunch observation highlights opportunity costs, not a claim that every free service hides fraud. Lindy is a survival heuristic sometimes applied to non-perishable things; it is not a general lifespan formula for people, firms or products.
Free lunch effect
Something appears to be free or beneficial, but often has hidden costs or trade-offs.
Lindy effect
The longer something has existed, the longer it is likely to continue existing.

sections.heading: Diminishing marginal returns
sections.body:
Concept clarified
This is a conditional production relationship: change one input while relevant others are fixed. It differs from returns to scale, where inputs change together.
Law of diminishing marginal returns
Adding more of one input, while keeping others constant, will eventually yield smaller increases in output.

sections.heading: Sustainability, contribution and profit
sections.body:
Concept clarified
“Sustainability law” and “profit law” are informal headings. Profit depends on how revenue and costs are defined. Price’s law is a contribution-concentration heuristic, not a universal workforce quota. Wages can reduce profit with everything else fixed, but productivity, demand and prices can also change; wages and profit are not inevitably inversely related.
Sustainability law
Balancing environmental, social, and economic needs for long-term development without depleting resources.
Price's law
A small percentage of contributors typically produce the majority of results in any field.
Profit law
Profit is the difference between total revenue and total costs in business operations.
The profits and wages law
An inverse relationship where higher wages can reduce profits and vice versa.

sections.heading: Prices, specialization and calculation
sections.body:
Concept clarified
The notes summarize an argument for decentralized price coordination. Market power, externalities, public goods and information problems qualify simple efficiency claims. The non-market calculation debate is a debate about information and allocation, not a proved impossibility of every public decision.
Division of labour within the free price system law
A free price system, the division of labour is guided by market prices, which allocate resources efficiently based on supply and demand.
Economic calculation law
Efficient resource allocation requires a pricing system in a competitive market to guide decisions.
Economic calculation outside business law
Resource allocation without market prices, such as in government or communal systems, faces efficiency challenges.

title: Economic models and evidence: distributions, regression and assumptions
summary: Know what a statistical tool can establish and which source entries are only labels.

sections.heading: SUR and GLS: identify the estimation problem
sections.body:
Concept clarified
SUR jointly models multiple regression equations and can exploit correlated errors across equations. GLS accounts for a specified error covariance structure; “estimate unknown parameters” alone does not distinguish it from other estimators. Neither method removes confounding automatically.
Measurement
Seemingly unrelated regression (SUR)
Linear regression model that consists of several regression equations
Generalised least squares (GLS)
Estimate the unknown parameters

sections.heading: Tails, normal distributions and missing symbols
sections.body:
Concept clarified
A long tail describes a distribution with many low-frequency values; it does not imply the distribution is normal. Bell curve and Gaussian normal distribution refer here to the same family. The source omits the parameter symbols: for a normal distribution, μ denotes the mean and σ the standard deviation.
Long tail
Many occurrences far from the "head" or central part of the distribution
Bell curve
The parameter is the mean or expectation of the distribution; and is its standard deviation

sections.heading: DSGE and Arrow–Debreu
sections.body:
Concept clarified
DSGE models combine dynamic decisions, stochastic shocks and equilibrium conditions. Results depend on specification and identification. Arrow–Debreu’s general-equilibrium framework requires conditions for existence and welfare results; the mere presence of contingent contracts does not ensure every real market is complete or efficient.
Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium (DSGE)
Aggregate economic phenomena, such as growth, business cycles, and policy effects, through the interaction of microeconomic agents under uncertainty over time.
Arrow-Debreu
General equilibrium in economics, demonstrating how markets for goods and securities can clear through the presence of a complete set of contingent contracts, thereby ensuring efficient allocation of resources.

sections.heading: Large numbers do not cure bad sampling
sections.body:
Concept clarified
A law of large numbers gives convergence results under specified conditions. More observations do not automatically repair biased collection, dependence or an undefined expectation.
Law of large numbers
As the number of trials or observations increases, the average result will get closer to the expected value.

sections.heading: Analysis is a practice, not a universal law
sections.body:
Concept clarified
The “analytics law” entry advocates systematic analysis but supplies no named result or evidence. Use data quality checks, competing explanations and uncertainty estimates instead of treating analysis as a guarantee.
Analytics law
Decisions come from systematically analysing data rather than relying on intuition alone.

sections.heading: A small mathematics index
sections.body:
Concept clarified
School, applied, pure and abstract mathematics are bare labels in the source. No syllabus, worked examples or additional content is present; the related statistics readings supply a useful next step without fabricating missing lessons.
Mathematics
School math
Applied math
Pure math
Abstract math

sections.heading: Gaussian and bell-curve terminology
sections.body:
Concept clarified
The truncated “Gaussian normal distributio” and “Bell curve” labels refer here to the same normal-distribution family, not a separate measurement method.
Gaussian normal distributio
Bell curve

title: Technology scaling: networks, speed, learning and organization
summary: Compare useful scaling models with loosely attributed “laws” and workplace satire.

sections.heading: Network-value heuristics
sections.body:
Concept clarified
Sarnoff, Metcalfe and Reed use different proxies for network value—audience, potential pairwise links and possible groups. Counting potential connections does not measure realized economic value; activity, costs and diminishing relevance matter.
Sarnoff’s law
The value of a broadcast network is proportional to the number of viewers.
Metcalfe’s law
The value of a network increases as the square of the number of its users grows.
Reed’s law
The value of a network grows exponentially as the number of possible subgroups or connections within the network increases.

sections.heading: Hardware, parallelism, learning and organizational design
sections.body:
Concept clarified
Moore’s observation concerns transistor scaling; it does not promise a doubling of useful application speed. Amdahl’s model limits speedup when a serial share remains. Wright’s learning relationship concerns unit cost and cumulative production, rather than elapsed time alone. Conway connects communication structures with system design.
Moore's law
The number of transistors on a microchip doubles approximately every two years, leading to increased computing power.
Amdahl's Law
The maximum improvement in performance of a system when only part of it is improved, highlighting diminishing returns for parallel processing.
Wright's law (learning curve)
As production increases, the cost per unit decreases due to efficiencies gained from experience.
Conway’s law
Organisations design systems that mirror their own communication structure.

sections.heading: A poorly attributed system-complexity claim
sections.body:
Unverified attribution and model
The source’s inverse-components “Gilbert’s law” claim has no provenance, definition of quality or supporting model. Fewer components can reduce coordination costs but can also hide complexity or remove necessary capability; no universal inverse law is established. This is not Gilbert’s Behaviour Engineering Model.
Gilbert's law
In system design,it states that the quality of a system is inversely proportional to the number of components in it.

title: Singapore land and planning: identify the site before using a number
summary: Read planning controls, use restrictions, plot ratio and land charges in their proper scope.

sections.heading: Site identity, property rights and building envelopes
sections.body:
Reviewed context; case-specific checks remain
The ministry list is a source filing system, not a sequence of approvals. Ownership can involve land, buildings, airspace and subterranean interests, but the title and legislation define the actual rights. The claims about 58 sites and universal 12 m/15.5 m heights are unverified; check the site’s planning controls rather than treating them as general rules.
Real Estate
Singapore Ministries
Ministry of Law (Minlaw)
Singapore Land Authority (SLA)
Landed areas have 58 sites without plot ratio
Consist of: land, air space, real property, subterranean, incorporeal hereditaments, corporeal hereditaments
2 storey height: 12m, 3 storey height: 15.5m

sections.heading: Housing types and dimensional controls
sections.body:
Reviewed context; case-specific checks remain
URA distinguishes GCBs, detached, semi-detached, terrace, strata-landed and apartment developments. Its landed controls include plot-size and width conditions: the notes’ 1,400 m²/18.5 m GCB, 400 m²/10 m detached and 200 m²/8 m semi-detached figures have recognizable contexts. They do not validate every coverage, height or property-size claim in this list. Shoebox and SOHO are not universal statutory area classes; Sentosa, strata and redevelopment cases need their own controls.
Good Class Bungalow, 1400m², 39 areas, 35% plot size and 18.5m width
Bungalow, 400m², 40% plot size and 10m width
Semi-Detach, 200m² and 8m width
Terrace House, 80m² and 6m width
Strata housing, townhouse, cluster housing. 40% plot size
Condominium, 4000m² and 40% plot size
High-rise apartment, 1000m² and more than 5 storey
Low-rise apartment, 1000m² and less than 6 storey
Service apartment
Sentosa Cove, 18,000 sf
Shoebox apartment, 70m²
Shop house is identified as multiple units

sections.heading: Commercial uses, conservation and ancillary facilities
sections.body:
Reviewed context; case-specific checks remain
Retail aisle widths, home-office fees, clinic/canteen/childcare limits and conservation classifications are preserved as unverified reference notes. Permitted use, fire safety, conservation and ancillary-use rules are separate checks; a stated size is not an automatic permission.
Retail unit, 50m². Single loaded, 2.0m-2.4m. Double loaded 2.4m-3.0m
Conservation areas: Little India, Boat Quay, Chinatown & Kampong Glam
Residential conservation areas: Blair Plain, Emerald Hill & Cairnhill
Small Office Home Office (SOHO) require home office permit, one-time $20
Clinics, 3000m², 20% GFA
Industrial canteen, 700m², 5% GFA
Childcare in Place of worship, 500m², 10% GFA

sections.heading: GFA, redevelopment and land betterment
sections.body:
Reviewed context; case-specific checks remain
GFA relates to site area and applicable gross plot ratio, subject to the current definition, exclusions and planning approval. Plot ratio is not a guaranteed storey entitlement. Reconstruction/A&A thresholds and loft treatment require the applicable handbook. Land Betterment Charge replaced Development Charge, Differential Premium and Temporary Development Levy from 1 August 2022; the old DP wording is historical. A TOL is not ownership or a guaranteed renewable tenancy.
Gross Floor Area (GFA) = plot ratio x site area
Plot ratio. 1.4: 5 sty, 1.6: 12 sty, 2.1: 24 sty, 2.8: 36 sty, >2.8: >36 sty
Loft = void area on ceiling
Redevelopment: 100%, reconstruction: >50%, alteration & addition: <50%
Government Land Sales Programme
Land Dealings (Approval) Unit, In-Principle Approval
Uses Differential premium
Able to issue Temporary Occupation License (TOL), bare, revocable, estoppel, coupled with grant & contractual

sections.heading: Plans, price regions and historical development charges
sections.body:
Reviewed context; case-specific checks remain
URA planning, developer controls and foreign-ownership approval are distinct functions. The Long-Term Plan and statutory Master Plan have different purposes; the old “Concept Plan” terminology and review intervals need their publication context. CCR/RCR/OCR and price indices are market-analysis classifications. The source’s development-charge arithmetic is not a current LBC assessment; check sector, use, baseline, valuation and effective rates.
Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA)
Housing and Developing Act
Sales of Commercial Properties Act
Residential Property Act
Qualifying Certificate, 5 years to Certificate of Statutory Completion (CSC), 2 years to sell the units, 8% tax increment yearly
Planning Act
Concept plan, 10 year revision, 40-50 years plan
Master plan, 5 years revision, 10-15 years plan
Development charge = development ceiling - development baseline
Development charge table of rates, revise every March and September
Cadastral map to show Lot based system, 30 Town-subdivision, 34 Mukim
Property Price Index (PPI)
Core Central Region (CCR), Rest of Central Region (RCR) & Outside Core Region (OCR)
Street block plan (e.g. setback)

title: Singapore title, tenure and property rights
summary: Separate registered ownership, caveats, easements, mortgages and statutory acquisition.

sections.heading: Registration, tenure and acquisition
sections.body:
Reviewed context; case-specific checks remain
A registered-title system differs from deeds registration. The source conflates caveat rules with a deeds-system definition: a caveat is a notice protecting a claimed interest, not ownership, and its duration and lapsing depend on the Land Titles Act. Mirror/curtain/insurance are explanatory principles rather than a guarantee against every defect. Leasehold, life estates, freehold and accessory lots require the actual register; acquisition compensation is a statutory assessment, not an assured market quote.
Information in Singapore Land Registry
State Land Act, chief valuer, commissioner of land
State Land Encroachment Act
Land Title Act
Land Title System have mirror, curtain and insurance principle
Registration of Deed Act, defeasible if there is caution or encumbrances e.g. caveat and have 5 years expiry
Deed system e.g. Will
Tenure: mode, estate: period
Leasehold, Life Estate, Freehold (Estate in Fee Simple or Estate in Perpetuity, Statutory Land Grant)
Accessory Lot (e.g. TS13-A12345K)
Land Acquisition Board, market value base on date of acquisition

sections.heading: Interests, fixtures and rights over neighbouring land
sections.body:
Reviewed context; case-specific checks remain
Distinguish legal/equitable interests, reversion, licences and proprietary rights. Fixture questions examine annexation and purpose. Easements and restrictive covenants have different functions; the source’s blanket 20-year/10-year-renewal statement is not verified as a universal rule. Creation, release, merger or court/statutory changes require the actual instrument and law. A statutory declaration does not itself transfer ownership.
Property Law
Common law, statutory law, equity
Legal interest, equitable interest, reversionary interest
Rights: possess, exclude, transfer, rent, collateral
Proprietary rights: binding / personal rights: license
Fixtures, fittings, chattels, trade chattels : measure by degree of annexation, purpose of annexation
Easement is for dominant tenement, restrictive covenant is for servient tenement and last for 20 years; renewable every 10 years
Easement creation: statutory law, right of water/electricity/light/way/support, express/implied, reservation, necessity, prescription
Easement removal: statutory, express release, implied, unification, court order
Oaths and Declaration Act, statutory declaration by the commissioner of oath

sections.heading: Bankruptcy and mortgage roles
sections.body:
Reviewed context; case-specific checks remain
The source confuses a bankruptcy filing debt threshold with the Debt Repayment Scheme. DRS assessment uses a total-debt ceiling of S$150,000 and additional criteria, not “below S$15,000”; it is not automatic admission or discharge. A mortgagor is the borrower/security provider; a mortgagee is the secured lender. Redemption normally concerns the mortgagor’s right to discharge the mortgage. The source’s automatic discharge timeline is not current individualized advice.
Bankruptcy Act, 15k min, <15k Debt Repayment Scheme (DRS), discharge 5 years, -2 years if paid, +2 for re lodge / repeat
Moneylenders Act
Mortgagor (borrower), mortgagee (have to rights to sell / redeem)

title: Owning property together: trusts, inheritance and decision authority
summary: Distinguish co-ownership, estate administration, trusts and powers to act.

sections.heading: LPA, trusts and inheritance
sections.body:
Reviewed context; case-specific checks remain
An LPA concerns authority after loss of mental capacity; it is not a will. Inter vivos and testamentary trusts arise in different circumstances; probate, letters of administration, Public Trustee functions and bankruptcy administration are not interchangeable. Resulting and constructive trusts cannot be reduced to “non-legal holding” or fraud alone. MUIS describes a wasiat generally limited to one-third for non-faraid beneficiaries, subject to the applicable rules; the source’s shorthand is incomplete.
(Lasting) Power of Attorney
Trust, trustee, trustor / settlor (Syriah law only allow 1/3 of asset to be willed)
Intervivo trust: during the person is alive, testamentary trust: dead/testate (grant of probate by executor), public trust: intestate or bankrupt (letter of administration by administrator)
Resulting trust: non legal holding, constructive trust: fraud, unregistered trust: temporary holding

sections.heading: REITs, gifts and co-ownership
sections.body:
Reviewed context; case-specific checks remain
“REIT is not heterogeneity” has no clear meaning or supporting explanation; it remains unresolved. A REIT is an investment vehicle, so use the related investing guide rather than equating units with direct ownership of a home. Gifts can require formalities and may be contested; “irrevocable” is not a sufficient legal test. Joint tenancy and tenancy-in-common differ, including survivorship and shares; the four unities are not an identical requirement for both.
Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) is not heterogeneity
Gift is voluntary, irrevocable and without consideration
Joint tenancy / tenancy-in-common (alienation, partitioning, court order): unity of possession, interest, title, time

title: Collective sales in Singapore: consent, procedure and disputes
summary: Understand why consent thresholds alone do not make an en-bloc sale valid.

sections.heading: Read the whole statutory process
sections.body:
Reviewed context; case-specific checks remain
The consent threshold is assessed by both share value and strata area, not share value alone. The 90%/80% distinction depends on the statutory development-age test; the notes omit the exact boundary and basis. A one-year consent-collection period is not a universal promise to finish every tender, application and transfer in one year. Committee rules, rescission, repeat attempts and objections have distinct procedures. The supplied quorum, waiting-period and cooling-off numbers are not independently validated here.
Land Title (Strata) Act
Collective sales (en-bloc), max. 1 year to complete through tender or auction
<10 years old 90% share value, >10 years old 80% of share value
Sales committee: 3-14 people, 30% of SV present, 20% to vote
5 days cooling off period
If you fail, wait 2 years. 1st attempt within 2 years 50% of SV, 2nd attempt 80% of SV
Appeal to Strata Title Board

title: Buying and selling property: contracts and conveyancing
summary: Follow authority, agreement, due diligence, completion and remedies without assuming every contract has the same clauses.

sections.heading: From negotiations to completion
sections.body:
Reviewed context; case-specific checks remain
Offer, acceptance, consideration and intention are starting concepts; property transactions also involve formalities and agreed conditions. “Subject to contract” affects intention but should not replace review of actual communications. Identify the parties, property, price, authority, deposit holder and requisitions. SAL conveyancing money arrangements are not the same as a developer’s project account. The source’s 2012 conditions, 8% rate and 21-day statement require the contract/version; they are not presented as universal current terms.
Contract Law
Subject to Contract will only bind in final agreement
Offer > acceptance > consideration > intention
Agreement must have property address, party name, price
Can be terminated by revocation, lapsed, counter offer, death, rejection
Stakeholder clause: conveyancing (CVY) account under Singapore Academy of Law
Requisitions with satisfactory replies from IRAS, PUB, BCA, URA, SMRT, LTA
The Law Society of Singapore's Condition of Sale 2012
Late completion interest: 8% p.a for both buyer and seller. Max. allowance is 21 days

sections.heading: Defects, invalidity, remedies and duties
sections.body:
Reviewed context; case-specific checks remain
Void and voidable transactions differ, but incapacity, mistake, misrepresentation and negligence require more precise legal tests than the source lists. Performance, frustration and breach are not all forms of successful completion; remedies depend on facts and law. Terms versus representations and conditions versus warranties cannot be decided solely by “official” versus “non-official” or “major” versus “minor.” The tort and waste labels remain study prompts rather than instructions to disclaim all premises liability.
Vitiating (void) factors: incapacity, mistake, illegality
Voidable: duress, undue influence, misrepresentation (innocent / contributory negligence, negligent, fraudulent / professional negligence)
Completed: performing, agreement, frustration, non-performance, seller bankrupt, Act of God, impossibility
Remedies: liquidated / unliquidated damages, specific performance, injunction
Caveat emptor, latent and patent defects
Torts of vicarious liability, negligence, defective of dangerous premises (disclaimer), waste (permissive, voluntary, equitable, ameliorating)
Privity of contract / estate
Conditions is major, warranty is minor
Expressed / implied terms is official, representation is non-official

sections.heading: Transport, lawful occupation and fire safety
sections.body:
Reviewed context; case-specific checks remain
A road-line reserve, lawful immigration status and fire-safety compliance are separate due-diligence checks. CEA provides rental checklists for identity and immigration checks; the source’s fine/jail figures are not verified as current penalties. The notes supply no fire-standard specification or site plan, so none is invented.
Ministry of Transport
Land Transport Authority (LTA)
Road Line Plan (reserve)
Ministry of Home Affair (MHA)
Immigration Act
Agent supposed to check passes, passport and validate
Anti-harbouring, max. fine 6k, jail 24 months
Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF)
Fire and safety standards

title: Developer purchases: licences, payment stages and prescribed terms
summary: Separate developer sales from private resale and check the exact prescribed agreement.

sections.heading: A developer sale is not a standard resale OTP
sections.body:
Reviewed context; case-specific checks remain
Developer licensing, sale/no-sale licences and prescribed forms are governed by the applicable regime. Compare the approved option and sale-and-purchase agreement, project-account rules, payment milestones, completion dates and defect clauses. A developer project account is not simply an SAL conveyancing account. The 75% booking-fee refund belongs to a specified unexercised prescribed option and conditions; it is not a general right to cancel every purchase. The source’s progressive percentages, 20%/5% “remorse,” 3% shortfall and late-interest figures require the actual form/version and are not independently endorsed.
Housing Developers (Control and Licensing) Act
>4 Units, same as commercial development
Sale-license, 1-4m paid up, require building plan approval
Uncompleted sale: booking fee 5% > exercise 15% > progressive 10,10,5,5,5,5,25% > 2% title transfer > 8% CSC > 5% after 1 year defect
No-sale license, only can sell after TOP
C2C selling: seller decides price > 1% OTP > exercise 4% or 9% > buyer stamp duty > requisitions & caveat
Project account under Singapore Academy of Law, can only withdraw for construction usage
Buyer fail to exercise: refund 75% of booking fee
Remorse buyer: refund 20% deposit, EC refund 5% of deposit
Shortfall compensation by developer: 3% allowance
Late completion by developer: 10% p.a. on instalment paid
Buyer late payment: 2% p.a. + prime rate
Advertising requires: track record, consent to change layout, name, license no., tenure, encumbrances, vacant possession, legal completion, lot base no.

title: Singapore property tax: annual value and use matter
summary: Distinguish recurring property tax from transaction duties and rental income tax.

sections.heading: Replace the old residential bands
sections.body:
Historical schedule replaced with current context
The residential schedules in the notes are historical. From 2025 the owner-occupied schedule begins with a zero-rated first S$12,000 of annual value; non-owner-occupied residential property follows a separate progressive schedule. Non-residential property generally uses a flat 10% of annual value. The note’s 5%-of-market-value land claim is not verified as a general rule. Annual value is not the sale price. Check the IRAS schedule, reliefs and billing/notification rules applicable to the property.
Ministry of Finance (MOF)
Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS)
Property Tax Act
Property tax to be prepaid by 31st January
Owner-occupied rate. 8k: 0%, 47k: 4%, every 15k +2% till 130k
Non-owner occupied rate. 30k: 10%, every 5k +2% till 90k
None residential property tax: 10% tax rate x annual value
Land/development tax: 5 % tax rate and market value
Notification: sales 1 month, succession 1 year, others 15 days

title: Property stamp duties: purchase, sale, leases and mortgages
summary: Identify the document, transaction date and buyer profile before choosing a duty schedule.

sections.heading: BSD and ABSD: old rates are unsafe
sections.body:
Historical rates corrected; check transaction date
Stamp duty applies to dutiable instruments, with deadlines depending on execution and receipt circumstances; a 14/30-day memory aid needs those conditions. Residential BSD has reached a 6% top marginal rate for acquisitions from 15 February 2023; the source’s 3% top rate is old. ABSD rates also changed: for individuals under the general rates effective 27 April 2023, SC first/second/third-or-later are 0/20/30%, PR 5/30/35%, and foreign buyers generally 60%, subject to rules and reliefs. FTA eligibility is not a blanket nationality exemption: the source incorrectly lists Ireland instead of Iceland, and eligibility depends on the qualifying treaty category.
Stamp Duty Act
Stamp duty is to stamp for documents only
14 days to stamp in SG, 30 days if not in SG
Buyer stamp duty. <180k: 1%, <360k 2% -1.8k, >360k, 3% - 5.4k
Additional buyer stamp duty (ABSD). SC: 0%, 7%, 10%+. SPR: 5%, 10%+. Others: 15%+
Remission: sell current property within 6 months or if you are from Switzerland, USA, Lichtenstein, Ireland, Norway

sections.heading: SSD, rental instruments, mortgages and penalties
sections.body:
Date-dependent duties; source terminology corrected
Residential SSD depends on acquisition date and holding period. The four-year 16/12/8/4% framework applies to acquisitions from 4 July 2025; the immediately preceding regime used a different holding period. Industrial SSD is a separate regime. Lease duty depends on term and rent, not a universal four-year charge for every lease. Ordinary mortgage duty of 0.4% capped at S$500 is duty on a mortgage instrument, not a bank application fee. For late stamping, the notes’ S$35 figure is wrong: IRAS states S$25 or four times the duty, whichever is greater, for lateness beyond three months; the shorter band also has a greater-of test.

sections.heading: BADIR: a workflow for a business question
sections.body:
Keep Business question, Analysis plan, Data collection, Insights and Recommendations connected. Specify population, period, granularity, validation and alternative explanations. An 80/20 cut or “shunting long tail” may discard important cases; document that choice and test its effect.
BADIR decision making
Business questions: what happened, why are you interested, what is the problem, when did it take place, where did it happen, who is impacted, what might have caused this, what do you think drive this
Analysis plan: analysis goal → hypotheses (criteria to prove or disprove) → methodology → data spec (determine level of granularity, assign unique ID, aggregate it) → project plan → kick-off meeting
Data collection: Data pull (define time period, shunting long tail: 80/20) > data cleansing and validation (univariate, cardinality, ratio and total, triangulation)
Insights: review pattern (is this a real problem, test vs control) > prove or disprove hypothesis (relationship between business question and hypothesis variable) > findings
Recommendations: actionable, based on key insights, supported by detailed findings

Key parts
Strategic Apex
Top management and its support staff. In school districts, this is the superintendent of schools and the administrative cabinet
Operative core
The workers who actually carry out the organization’s tasks. Teachers constitute the operative core in schools
Middle line
middle-and-lower-level management. Principals are the middle-level managers in school districts
Technostructure
Analysts such as engineers, accountants, planners, researchers, and personnel managers. In school districts, divisions such as instruction, business, personnel, public relations, research and development, and the like constitute the technostructure
Support staff
The people who provide indirect services. In school districts, similar services include maintenance, clerical, food service, busing, legal counsel, and consulting to provide support
Prime coordinating mechanism
Direct supervision
That one individual is responsible of the work of others
Standardisation of work process
Exists when the content of work is specified or programmed. In schools, this refers to job descriptions that govern the work performance of educators
Standardisation of skills
Exists when the kind of training necessary to do the work is specified. In school systems, this refers to state certificates required for the various occupants of a school’s hierarchy
Standardisation of output
Exists when the results of the work are specified. Examples include competency testing of teachers, state-mandated testing of students, state-mandated curriculum, prescriptive learning objectives, and other efforts toward legislated learning
Mutual adjustment
Exists when work is coordinated through informal communication
Type of decentralisation
Vertical decentralisation
The distribution of power down the chain of command, or shared authority between managers and subordinates in any organisation
Horizontal decentralisation
The extent to which non administrators (including staff) make decisions, or shared authority between line and staff
Selective decentralisation
The extent to which decision-making power is delegated to different units within the organisation

title: Business ethics: compare the reasons for a decision

sections.heading: Ethics concerns conduct and reasons
sections.body:
Editorial clarification
The supplied definitions concern right and wrong in business decisions, what organizations ought to do, and how policy and conduct reveal their stance. Compliance sets obligations, but a definition of ethics solely as exceeding the minimum is too narrow: respecting existing duties is also ethically significant. The quotations are retained with the source’s abbreviated attributions; complete editions/page references are not supplied.
Ethics
“The study of business situations, activities and decisions where issues of right and wrong are addressed”(Crane and Matten).
Business ethics is about what business organisations OUGHT to do – and inevitably this brings us into the realm of 'value judgements'.
Ultimately it is the behaviour of organisations (their policies and actions) that determine the ethical stance of an organisation.
"The ethical stance is the extent to which an organisation will exceed its minimum obligations to stakeholders and society at large" (Johnson & Scholes).

sections.heading: A map of ethical perspectives
sections.body:

Editorial clarification
The claim that ethics cannot be taught is a view to examine, not an established educational result. “Leave ethics to government” is an incomplete description of Friedman. Privacy, working conditions, technology, environment and cross-border conduct create practical responsibilities. Volkswagen and Cambridge Analytica are historical cases with dated records, not grounds for a blanket claim about every present activity of the companies. The News Corporation example lacks a specific case/date in the notes and remains an incomplete historical prompt.

The supplied checklist asks about law, values, conscience, public exposure and persistent questioning. Its attribution is retained as a historical source claim, not authenticated as the complete current TI code. TI’s official document sets out a broader set of principles, including responsible practices, privacy, conflicts, respect and use of resources. The newspaper test is a prompt for accountability, not a rule that publicity or embarrassment alone decides what is right.

sections.heading: Eight psychosocial themes and associated strengths
sections.body:
The source lists age-period labels, tensions and virtues. People’s development and cultures vary; the outline is not a validated assessment of a particular reader or a substitute for an individual psychological evaluation.
Erikson’s psychosocial life cycle
Infancy: trust vs mistrust, hope
Early childhood: autonomy vs shame, will
Play age: initiative vs guilt, purpose
School age: industry vs inferiority, competence
Adolescence: identity vs confusion, fidelity
Young adulthood: intimacy vs isolation, love
Adulthood/maturity: generativity vs stagnation, care
Old age: integrity vs despair: wisdom

sections.heading: Manufacturing process options
sections.body:
The notes associate project/job-shop/batch/line/continuous work with different volume patterns. These are typical teaching distinctions, not a rule that every continuous operation is fully automated.
Manufacturing processes
Ad-hoc project: one-off
Job shop: low volume
Batch: mid volume
Line: large volume
Continuous: automated

sections.heading: Flow time, WIP and throughput
sections.body:
Editorial clarification
For a stable flow system with consistent averages and boundary, Little’s relationship can be written average WIP = average throughput rate × average flow time. Rearranging gives flow time = WIP / throughput rate when the rate is positive. Units must agree: items divided by items/hour gives hours. Rated capacity is not automatically achieved throughput, so the source’s “capacity” parenthesis is unsafe as a substitution. Manage the constraint rather than optimizing every activity independently.
Measure process
Flow: performance per period
Capacity: production per resource
Throughput time (flow) = work in progress (inventory) / throughput rate (capacity)
Theory of constraints: effort should be made to manage to the narrowest point in a system

sections.heading: Service process options
sections.body:
Professional service, service shop and mass service compare customization/variety and volume. They are idealized patterns; actual offerings can combine them.
Service-sector processes
Professional: high variety, low volume
Service shop: customisation with limit
Mass: no customisation
